title: PCA answer-length fix and explanation gaps (200 questions)

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A global retailer sells limited-edition products online in North America, Europe, and Asia. Inventory counts must never be oversold, even when customers on different continents buy the last unit at the same moment. The inventory database must scale horizontally during launches and survive the loss of an entire region with no data loss. Which database design should the architect choose?
options: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with high availability and cross-region read replicas deployed across all three continents.
Cloud Spanner with a multi-region instance configuration, giving synchronous, strongly consistent cross-region replication of inventory.
Cloud Bigtable with replication across three regions and multi-cluster routing policies.
Firestore in Datastore mode with a multi-region location and strongly consistent reads.
questions.correct_rationale: Spanner provides externally consistent, horizontally scalable transactions across regions with synchronous replication, preventing overselling and surviving a regional loss with zero RPO. Cloud SQL replicas are asynchronous and writes go to one primary, Bigtable replication is eventually consistent, and Firestore isn't designed for high-throughput relational inventory transactions across continents.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud SQL replicas are asynchronous and writes go to one primary, so overselling is possible; Bigtable replication is eventually consistent; Firestore isn't designed for high-throughput relational inventory transactions.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A media company must exit its colocation data center within six months when the lease ends. It runs 300 VMware VMs hosting a mix of legacy applications. Leadership wants minimal risk and no application changes during the move, followed by gradual modernization afterward. What migration approach should the architect recommend first?
options: Refactor all 300 applications into microservices on GKE before the lease deadline.
Rewrite the applications as containerized Cloud Run services running on fully managed infrastructure.
Retire half the applications and rebuild the remaining services using serverless computing patterns.
Rehost the VMs to Compute Engine using Migrate to Virtual Machines, then modernize incrementally.
questions.correct_rationale: A tight deadline with no application changes favors rehosting, and Migrate to Virtual Machines automates moving VMs to Compute Engine with testing and cutover.
questions.distractor_summary: Refactoring or rewriting 300 applications in six months carries high risk, and retiring applications requires analysis that doesn't fit the stated deadline.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A fintech company runs 40 microservices. Some are stateless APIs, others are stateful services that require persistent volumes, and several use sidecar containers and Kubernetes-native tooling such as Helm and operators. The small platform team doesn't want to manage nodes, upgrades, or capacity. Which compute platform should the architect choose?
options: GKE Autopilot with Google-managed nodes and automatic capacity scaling.
Cloud Run for all services with fully managed container infrastructure.
Compute Engine managed instance groups with autoscaling policies.
GKE Standard with manually sized and operationally managed node pools.
questions.correct_rationale: Autopilot runs Kubernetes workloads, including stateful sets and Helm-based tooling, while Google manages nodes and capacity.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Run doesn't provide the full Kubernetes API for operators and persistent volumes, MIGs lack Kubernetes tooling, and GKE Standard requires node management.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A logistics company collects GPS readings from 500,000 trucks every five seconds. A customer-facing app must show each truck's latest positions with millisecond latency, while analysts run SQL over years of history. The company wants managed services throughout. Which architecture fits best?
options: Trucks write GPS readings directly to Cloud SQL, and analysts query the cross-region read replicas.
Pub/Sub ingests readings into BigQuery, and the customer-facing app queries BigQuery for current positions.
Pub/Sub for ingestion, Dataflow for processing, Bigtable for low-latency serving, and BigQuery for analytics.
Cloud Storage for raw GPS files, with the app reading the latest position files directly from buckets.
questions.correct_rationale: Pub/Sub and Dataflow handle high-volume streaming, Bigtable serves low-latency key-based lookups, and BigQuery handles large-scale SQL analytics.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud SQL can't absorb this write rate, BigQuery isn't designed for millisecond serving to many users, and reading files from Cloud Storage isn't suitable for low-latency app queries.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A European healthcare startup must keep all patient data in the EU. Its US-based analytics team needs to run reports on that data, and European clinicians need low-latency access to the application. How should the architect design the data placement?
options: Store patient data in US multi-region BigQuery where analysts query it, and replicate a synchronized copy to EU regions for clinicians.
Deploy the application and data stores in EU regions, let US analysts query EU BigQuery remotely, and enforce EU locations with org policies.
Store all patient data in EU regions and export nightly encrypted extracts to US Cloud Storage buckets for the analytics team.
Use globally distributed BigQuery and Cloud Storage resources, since Google Cloud encrypts all data at rest and in transit by default.
questions.correct_rationale: Keeping data stores and datasets in EU locations satisfies residency, and analysts can query EU datasets from anywhere without moving data, with location constraints enforcing the rule.
questions.distractor_summary: Copying or exporting data to the US violates residency, and encryption doesn't replace location requirements.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: An e-commerce platform's order service calls inventory, payment, and email services synchronously. During flash sales, slowness in the email service causes order submissions to time out, even though email isn't critical to completing the order. What architectural change should the architect recommend?
options: Increase the order service's synchronous timeout to five minutes for all downstream calls.
Scale the email service vertically by upgrading it to larger machine types with more CPU and memory.
Merge all services into a single monolithic application that keeps the same synchronous calls.
Publish order events to Pub/Sub and have the email service consume them asynchronously.
questions.correct_rationale: Decoupling non-critical downstream work through Pub/Sub absorbs spikes and prevents slow consumers from blocking the critical path.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer timeouts worsen user experience, vertical scaling doesn't remove the coupling, and a monolith reduces independent scalability.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: An engineering firm runs simulation workloads in its data center, but peaks at quarter end exceed on-premises capacity. The firm wants to burst to Google Cloud using the same container images, deployment tooling, and policies it uses on-premises, over a private, high-bandwidth connection. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use Dedicated Interconnect and GKE Enterprise to manage on-premises and cloud clusters as one fleet.
Use HA VPN for private connectivity and rewrite the simulation workloads as Cloud Run functions.
Copy simulation data to Cloud Storage buckets and run the workloads on BigQuery.
Purchase additional on-premises hardware to handle the quarter-end peak capacity demands.
questions.correct_rationale: Dedicated Interconnect provides private high-bandwidth connectivity, and GKE Enterprise allows consistent management of clusters across environments, enabling bursting with the same tooling.
questions.distractor_summary: Rewriting for functions changes the application, BigQuery isn't a simulation platform, and more hardware sits idle outside peaks.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company is moving an event streaming platform to Google Cloud. Dozens of existing producers and consumers use Apache Kafka client libraries and Kafka Connect, and rewriting them isn't feasible. The operations team doesn't want to run Kafka brokers or ZooKeeper. What should the architect recommend?
options: Pub/Sub with all producer and consumer clients rewritten to the Pub/Sub API.
Self-managed Apache Kafka running on Compute Engine instances.
Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka clusters.
Cloud Tasks queues for asynchronous task dispatch and retries.
questions.correct_rationale: Managed Service for Apache Kafka provides Kafka-compatible clusters without managing brokers, preserving existing clients and connectors.
questions.distractor_summary: Pub/Sub requires rewriting clients, self-managed Kafka adds operations work, and Cloud Tasks is for task dispatch, not event streaming.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A marketing agency hosts a static single-page application with global users. It wants low latency worldwide, a custom domain with HTTPS, and the lowest operational effort and cost, with no servers. What should the architect design?
options: A Compute Engine managed instance group in each region running Nginx as the web server tier.
A Cloud Storage bucket behind a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN and managed SSL.
GKE Autopilot with an Ingress resource, managed SSL certificates, and Cloud CDN enabled globally.
Cloud Run deployed in a single region without Cloud CDN, global load balancing, or edge caching.
questions.correct_rationale: Serving static assets from Cloud Storage through a global load balancer with Cloud CDN gives global low latency, HTTPS on a custom domain, and no servers.
questions.distractor_summary: VMs and GKE add management, and a single-region Cloud Run service without CDN adds latency for distant users.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A bank runs hundreds of nightly Apache Spark ETL jobs on an on-premises Hadoop cluster. It wants to move to Google Cloud with minimal code changes and no cluster management, paying only while jobs run. What should the architect recommend?
options: Rewrite all the Spark jobs as BigQuery SQL scheduled queries.
Run Spark on a permanently provisioned GKE Standard cluster.
Use Dataflow with the Apache Spark runner extension for the nightly jobs.
Use Google Cloud Dataproc Serverless for Apache Spark.
questions.correct_rationale: Serverless Spark runs existing Spark jobs without provisioning or managing clusters and bills only for job execution.
questions.distractor_summary: Rewriting in SQL is a large effort, a permanent GKE cluster requires management and idle cost, and Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines rather than Spark jobs.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A retail company trained a demand-forecasting model and needs to serve online predictions to its ordering system with autoscaling, versioned deployments, and monitoring for prediction drift. The data science team doesn't want to manage serving infrastructure. What should the architect recommend?
options: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint for online prediction with model monitoring.
Package the trained model in a custom VM image and run it behind a managed instance group.
Run predictions as a nightly BigQuery ML batch job that precomputes all possible order forecasts.
Store the serialized model in Cloud Storage and load it separately in each client ordering application.
questions.correct_rationale: Vertex AI endpoints provide managed, autoscaled online serving with versioning and model monitoring.
questions.distractor_summary: MIGs require managing serving infrastructure, precomputing all predictions isn't feasible for online requests, and loading models in clients complicates updates and monitoring.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A payments company consumes a fraud-scoring service from a SaaS vendor that runs on Google Cloud. The company's security team prohibits internet paths and VPC peering with third parties, and the vendor's internal ranges overlap with the company's. How should the architect connect them?
options: Create an HA VPN tunnel between the company VPC and the vendor's VPC with non-overlapping ranges.
Set up VPC Network Peering with export custom route filters to share routes safely.
The vendor publishes the service with Private Service Connect; the company creates a PSC endpoint.
Use Cloud NAT to route traffic to the vendor's public API endpoint over the internet.
questions.correct_rationale: Private Service Connect offers private, service-level access across organizations without peering, and overlapping ranges don't matter because consumers use their own endpoint IP. VPN and peering require non-overlapping routes and network-level connectivity, and Cloud NAT uses the internet.
questions.distractor_summary: VPN and peering require non-overlapping routes and network-level connectivity, which the overlapping ranges prevent; Cloud NAT uses the internet, violating the security requirement.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A logistics company wants to expose shipment-tracking APIs to hundreds of external partners, with developer onboarding through a portal, API keys, per-partner quotas, usage analytics, and the option to charge partners in the future. What should the architect recommend?
options: Cloud Endpoints deployed on Cloud Run for API key validation and quotas.
Apigee API management with developer portal, quotas, analytics, and monetization.
A global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor rate limiting rules.
API keys hardcoded in partner applications calling a Cloud Run backend service.
questions.correct_rationale: Apigee provides full API lifecycle management, including developer portals, quotas, analytics, and monetization.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Endpoints offers lighter management without these partner program features, and load balancers or hardcoded keys don't provide API product management.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A data engineering team has 150 existing Apache Airflow DAGs that orchestrate BigQuery, Dataproc, and external API jobs with complex dependencies. It wants to move orchestration to Google Cloud with minimal rework and a managed service. What should the architect recommend?
options: Rewrite all 150 DAGs as Google Cloud Workflows definitions with YAML.
Cloud Scheduler with one scheduled job per individual task in the pipeline.
Pub/Sub triggers chained between each task to manage the dependencies.
Cloud Composer running managed Apache Airflow with the existing DAGs.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Composer is managed Apache Airflow, so existing DAGs can run with minimal changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Rewriting as Workflows is significant rework, and Cloud Scheduler or Pub/Sub chains don't handle complex dependency graphs well.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A web application runs on a regional managed instance group behind a load balancer. User sessions are stored in each VM's memory, so users are logged out whenever autoscaling removes a VM. The team wants stateless VMs without changing the login flow. What should the architect recommend?
options: Store session data in a Memorystore for Redis instance shared by all VMs in the group.
Enable client IP session affinity on the load balancer and disable autoscaling entirely.
Store session data on each VM's local SSD and replicate it across instances manually.
Increase the instance group's minimum number of instances to prevent any scale-in events.
questions.correct_rationale: Externalizing sessions to a managed in-memory store lets any instance serve any user and makes VMs disposable.
questions.distractor_summary: Affinity with no autoscaling sacrifices elasticity, local SSD data is lost with the VM, and a larger minimum size doesn't prevent scale-in losses.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A B2B SaaS company is onboarding enterprise customers who require strong isolation of their data and compute, separate audit trails, and per-customer cost reporting. The company expects about 200 customers. Which tenancy design should the architect recommend?
options: Use one shared project for all tenants, with separation by resource labels and naming conventions.
Create one VPC network per tenant inside a single shared project with firewall rules.
A dedicated project per tenant from a template under a tenants folder with inherited policies.
Create a separate Google Cloud organization per tenant with independent admin accounts and billing.
questions.correct_rationale: Projects are strong boundaries for IAM, quotas, audit logs, and billing, and automation plus folder-level policies make 200 projects manageable.
questions.distractor_summary: Labels and VPCs in a shared project don't isolate IAM or audit trails, and separate organizations make central governance very difficult.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: An online retailer wants to minimize the scope of its PCI DSS assessment. Only the payment service handles cardholder data; dozens of other services don't. How should the architect design the environment?
options: Keep all services in one VPC and apply strict firewall rules between service tiers.
Isolate the payment service in dedicated projects and a separate network, with VPC-SC and tokenization.
Encrypt all services' data with CMEK and keep them in the same VPC with shared IAM bindings and logging.
Place all services in a single Shared VPC with the same IAM bindings and a common audit logging configuration.
questions.correct_rationale: Isolating cardholder data into its own projects and network, with tokenization for other systems, shrinks the in-scope environment for PCI assessments.
questions.distractor_summary: Shared networks and IAM keep everything in scope, and encryption alone doesn't reduce scope.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A US hospital network plans to store and process protected health information (PHI) on Google Cloud. What should the architect ensure first from a compliance standpoint?
options: Use only Google Cloud regions located within the hospital's home state or geographic area.
Enable customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) on every service that stores data.
Store protected health information only in Cloud Storage with access logging and retention policies.
Execute a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with Google and use only HIPAA-covered services.
questions.correct_rationale: Under HIPAA, a BAA must be in place and PHI should be limited to covered services, with customers responsible for configuring them securely.
questions.distractor_summary: State-level regions aren't a HIPAA requirement, CMEK is a supporting control rather than a prerequisite, and restricting to one service is unnecessary.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A European government agency requires that its workloads run only in EU regions, that support personnel access is restricted to EU persons, and that these controls are enforced automatically with minimal custom configuration. What should the architect recommend?
options: Deploy Assured Workloads with an EU sovereign controls package on the agency's folder.
Apply organization policy location constraints restricting resources to EU regions only.
Configure VPC Service Controls perimeters around all projects in the organization.
Create separate billing accounts for each region with independent access controls.
questions.correct_rationale: Assured Workloads applies compliance packages that enforce data location, personnel access restrictions, and related controls for a folder.
questions.distractor_summary: Location constraints alone don't control personnel access, VPC Service Controls limits data exfiltration rather than sovereignty, and billing accounts don't enforce compliance.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A bank's regulator requires that encryption keys protecting customer data in BigQuery and Cloud Storage be generated and held in an external key management system outside Google's infrastructure, so the bank can deny access to its data at any time. What should the architect use?
options: Rely on Google default encryption for data at rest in BigQuery and Cloud Storage with no extra configuration.
Use CMEK with Cloud KMS software keys stored in a Google-managed key ring in the same project.
Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM) with keys held in an external key management system.
Use customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK) when writing data to BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud EKM uses keys stored and managed in a third-party key management system outside Google, letting the bank revoke access.
questions.distractor_summary: Default encryption and Cloud KMS keep keys within Google, and CSEK isn't supported for BigQuery.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company wants CMEK for its application data. The security team must control key rotation and access, while application teams must not be able to destroy or change keys, and security must not be able to read application data. How should the architect design key management?
options: Create keys in each application project and grant application teams the Cloud KMS Admin role on them.
Create key rings in a security project, and grant each service agent encrypt/decrypt on only the keys it needs.
Use one shared encryption key for all applications, with rotation handled by the application teams.
Use Google-managed encryption keys and restrict data access through IAM policies on each project.
questions.correct_rationale: A central key project separates key administration from data access, and granting encrypt/decrypt only to service agents enforces separation of duties.
questions.distractor_summary: Giving app teams KMS Admin lets them destroy keys, a shared key increases blast radius, and Google-managed keys don't meet the CMEK requirement.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: Developers store database passwords and API tokens in environment variables and configuration files in Git. Security wants credentials centrally stored, access-controlled per application, audited, and rotated without redeploying code. What should the architect recommend?
options: Encrypt the configuration files with a shared encryption key stored in the repository.
Store secrets in a private Cloud Storage bucket with IAM access controls and audit logging enabled.
Store secrets as values in Cloud KMS keys, with per-application key rings, access policies, and audit logging.
Store secrets in Secret Manager with per-secret IAM, runtime references, and rotation schedules.
questions.correct_rationale: Secret Manager stores secrets with per-secret IAM, audit logging, versioning, and rotation support.
questions.distractor_summary: Shared encryption keys and buckets lack secret-specific controls, and Cloud KMS manages encryption keys rather than storing arbitrary secrets.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company's workforce identities live in Microsoft Entra ID. Security doesn't want to synchronize user accounts into Cloud Identity, but employees must access the Google Cloud console and APIs using their Entra ID credentials with group-based access. What should the architect implement?
options: Workforce Identity Federation with Entra ID as the IdP, granting roles to federated workforce principals.
Google Cloud Directory Sync to periodically synchronize all user accounts from Entra ID into Cloud Identity.
Create a separate service account for each employee and distribute its key through a secure password vault.
Create duplicate Google accounts matching the Entra ID users with the same passwords and group memberships.
questions.correct_rationale: Workforce Identity Federation lets external IdP users access Google Cloud without synchronizing identities into Cloud Identity, with IAM granted to federated principals.
questions.distractor_summary: GCDS synchronizes users, service accounts aren't for people, and duplicate accounts create security and management issues.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company wants contractors on personal laptops to access internal web applications hosted on Google Cloud without a VPN, but only when their device meets security requirements and they authenticate with MFA. What should the architect design?
options: Make the internal web applications public with strong passwords, rate limiting, and IP-based restrictions.
Deploy a VPN concentrator on Compute Engine and require contractors to connect before they reach any app.
Place the applications behind Identity-Aware Proxy with Access Context Manager enforcing device posture.
Use Cloud Armor IP allowlists for each contractor's home IP address and require MFA at the app layer too.
questions.correct_rationale: IAP enforces identity-based access to applications, and access levels add context such as device state, implementing zero-trust access without VPN. Public apps expose attack surface, VPN contradicts the requirement, and home IP allowlists are fragile and don't check devices.
questions.distractor_summary: Public apps expose attack surface; VPN contradicts the no-VPN requirement; home IP allowlists are fragile and don't verify device posture.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company loads customer support transcripts into BigQuery for analytics. Legal requires that credit card numbers and national ID numbers in the transcripts be detected and masked before analysts see the data. What should the architect use?
options: BigQuery column-level encryption with customer-managed encryption keys on the sensitive columns.
Sensitive Data Protection to inspect and de-identify the transcripts in the ingestion pipeline.
VPC Service Controls perimeters around BigQuery to prevent data exfiltration to unauthorized users.
IAM roles restricting analysts to specific tables and views that exclude the sensitive columns.
questions.correct_rationale: Sensitive Data Protection detects and de-identifies sensitive data such as card numbers and IDs within free-form text.
questions.distractor_summary: Encryption and VPC Service Controls protect data but don't mask values inside text, and IAM controls table access rather than content.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company is creating its Google Cloud foundation. It wants preventive guardrails that apply to every current and future project, such as restricting resource locations, blocking public buckets, and blocking service account keys, while allowing documented exceptions. What should the architect implement?
options: Detective controls through Cloud Monitoring log alerts that notify the team on policy violations after the fact.
Manual security reviews of each new project by the platform team before granting any team access to its resources.
VPC firewall rules in every VPC to restrict network access to approved destinations and ports.
Organization policy constraints at the org and folder levels, with project-level exceptions where approved.
questions.correct_rationale: Organization policies are preventive controls inherited by all resources, with exceptions set at lower levels when approved.
questions.distractor_summary: Log alerts detect violations after they happen, manual reviews don't scale, and firewall rules don't govern resource configuration.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: An internal reporting application has an RTO of 12 hours and an RPO of 24 hours. The business wants the lowest-cost disaster recovery plan that protects against a regional outage. What should the architect choose?
options: Backup and restore: daily backups stored in another region, with infrastructure recreated from templates.
Warm standby in a second region with scaled-down infrastructure running continuously at reduced capacity.
Active-active across two regions with full-scale infrastructure and load balancing between both regions.
Synchronous replication of all data to a second region with automatic failover for every service.
questions.correct_rationale: Relaxed RTO and RPO fit backup and restore, which is the cheapest DR pattern because no standby infrastructure runs.
questions.distractor_summary: Warm standby, active-active, and synchronous replication cost more and exceed the requirements.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A customer-facing application uses Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in `us-central1` with HA enabled. The business now requires recovery within 30 minutes and at most a few minutes of data loss if the entire region fails. What should the architect add?
options: More frequent automated backups with point-in-time recovery enabled in the same region.
A second HA standby instance in another availability zone within the us-central1 region for zone failures.
A cross-region read replica that can be promoted during an outage, with a documented failover process.
An hourly export to Cloud Storage with automated restore scripts for disaster recovery scenarios.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-region replicas replicate asynchronously with low lag and can be promoted quickly, meeting minute-level RPO and a short RTO for regional failure.
questions.distractor_summary: Same-region backups or standbys don't survive a regional outage, and hourly exports give up to an hour of data loss plus slow restores.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A global payments company requires that its API remain available with no loss of committed transactions even if an entire region fails, and it wants traffic served from multiple regions simultaneously. Which architecture should the architect choose?
options: Active-passive deployment with Cloud SQL and a cross-region read replica that can be promoted during a failover event.
Active-active application instances in multiple regions behind a global load balancer, with Spanner multi-region.
Single-region GKE cluster with regional persistent disks and daily backups to Cloud Storage.
Pilot light in a second region with daily backups and infrastructure templates ready to deploy quickly.
questions.correct_rationale: Global load balancing across active regions combined with Spanner's synchronous multi-region replication provides zero RPO and continuous availability.
questions.distractor_summary: Active-passive and pilot light designs have failover delays and possible data loss, and a single region can't survive a regional outage.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A company runs a stateful application on Compute Engine VMs with persistent disks in `europe-west1`. It needs a warm standby in `europe-west4` with an RPO of about one minute and an RTO under an hour, without rewriting the application. What should the architect design?
options: Daily persistent disk snapshots copied to Cloud Storage in europe-west4 with documented manual restore and validation procedures.
Regional persistent disks that span both europe-west1 and europe-west4, with synchronous replication between the two.
A machine image created weekly and stored in a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket for later disaster recovery restores.
Persistent Disk Asynchronous Replication to europe-west4, with a standby MIG attaching secondary disks on failover.
questions.correct_rationale: Persistent Disk Asynchronous Replication provides cross-region disk replication with an RPO around one minute, and a pre-created standby environment supports a fast RTO. Daily snapshots and weekly images miss the RPO, and regional persistent disks span zones within a single region, not two regions.
questions.distractor_summary: Daily snapshots and weekly machine images miss the one-minute RPO; regional persistent disks span zones within a single region, not across two regions.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A company runs a critical microservices platform on a single regional GKE cluster in `us-east1`. The business now requires the service to survive a full regional outage with an RTO of minutes. What should the architect recommend?
options: Deploy a second GKE cluster in a different region, with multi-cluster Gateway routing and replicated data stores for failover.
Increase the number of nodes in the existing regional cluster to handle higher traffic loads during peak events.
Convert the existing cluster to GKE Autopilot so Google manages node capacity and availability.
Add a node pool in a second availability zone within the same us-east1 region for redundancy.
questions.correct_rationale: A regional cluster survives zonal failures but not regional ones, so a second cluster in another region with global multi-cluster routing and replicated data is needed.
questions.distractor_summary: More nodes, Autopilot, or another zone don't protect against losing the region.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: An ad-tech company serves user profiles from Bigtable in `us-central1` with single-digit-millisecond reads. It needs automatic failover to another region if the primary becomes unavailable, and it accepts eventual consistency for reads. What should the architect configure?
options: Daily Bigtable backups copied to a Cloud Storage bucket in another region for failover restores.
A Cloud SQL read replica populated from the Bigtable data through periodic batch exports.
Bigtable replication with clusters in two regions and multi-cluster routing in the app profile.
Export Bigtable data to BigQuery and serve failover reads from the BigQuery dataset directly in the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Bigtable replication keeps clusters in multiple regions in sync, and multi-cluster routing automatically sends requests to the nearest available cluster.
questions.distractor_summary: Backups require restore time, and Cloud SQL or BigQuery can't serve the same low-latency workload.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A company must back up hundreds of Compute Engine VMs, Cloud SQL instances, and GKE workloads with centralized policies, and it needs backups that can't be deleted or modified by anyone, including administrators, before retention expires, to protect against ransomware. What should the architect recommend?
options: Snapshot schedules on each persistent disk, with retention locked at the project level by an organization policy.
Backup and DR Service with backup vaults configured with enforced retention for immutability.
Nightly exports to a Cloud Storage bucket with Object Versioning and retention policies enabled.
Machine images created by a Cloud Scheduler job and stored in a separate admin-only project for safekeeping.
questions.correct_rationale: Backup and DR Service centrally manages backups across services, and backup vaults with enforced retention make backups immutable until retention ends.
questions.distractor_summary: Snapshots, exports, and machine images can be deleted by privileged users, and versioning alone doesn't prevent deletion.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A web application runs in a zonal managed instance group in `us-west1-a`. During a zonal incident, the application was down for hours, violating its 99.95% availability target. What change best addresses this with minimal redesign?
options: Convert to a regional managed instance group spread across multiple zones behind the load balancer.
Use a larger machine type to handle more traffic during a zonal incident or failover event.
Add a second zonal managed instance group in the same availability zone for added redundancy and capacity.
Enable autohealing health checks on the existing instance group to restart any failed instances quickly.
questions.correct_rationale: Regional MIGs distribute instances across zones so that the application survives a zonal failure.
questions.distractor_summary: Larger machines and more instances in the same zone don't add zone resilience, and autohealing can't recreate VMs in a failed zone.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A company runs a content management system that needs a shared NFS file system for many VMs. The file system must remain available if a zone fails, without the team managing replication. What should the architect choose?
options: A single persistent disk shared in read-only mode across all the VMs in the project.
Filestore Basic HDD tier with a single zonal instance mounted by all the VMs.
Filestore Enterprise (regional) tier providing NFS across multiple zones automatically.
Local SSDs on each VM synchronized with rsync across instances on a regular schedule.
questions.correct_rationale: Filestore Enterprise provides a regional NFS service that replicates across zones and survives zonal failure.
questions.distractor_summary: Read-only disks don't support writes from many VMs, Basic tier instances are zonal, and rsync on local SSDs is fragile.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A company's primary customer portal runs on-premises, with a standby deployment on Google Cloud. It wants DNS to automatically direct users to the Google Cloud deployment when the on-premises endpoint fails health checks, and back when it recovers. What should the architect configure?
options: A manual DNS change runbook that the operations team executes during a service outage.
Cloud DNS failover routing policy with health checks and a Google Cloud backup endpoint.
Cloud CDN caching in front of the on-premises endpoint to absorb traffic during failures.
Cloud NAT for on-premises traffic with automatic failover to the Google Cloud deployment.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud DNS routing policies with health checking can fail over between primary and backup targets automatically.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual runbooks slow recovery, Cloud CDN doesn't fail over dynamic applications to a different backend by itself, and Cloud NAT handles outbound traffic.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Designing for high availability and disaster recovery
questions.question: A company's BigQuery data warehouse in the `US` multi-region powers critical daily reporting. Leadership wants the warehouse to be able to continue operating from a secondary region if the primary becomes unavailable, with managed replication and a controlled failover. What should the architect recommend?
options: Nightly exports to Cloud Storage in another region with automated restore scripts.
Copy datasets manually to another region each week using the BigQuery console or CLI tools.
Rely on BigQuery's in-region durability and multi-zone replication for availability.
BigQuery cross-region dataset replication with managed failover in a secondary region.
questions.correct_rationale: BigQuery's cross-region replication and managed disaster recovery replicate datasets and support failover to a secondary region.
questions.distractor_summary: Exports and weekly copies have large RPOs and manual recovery, and in-region durability doesn't address regional unavailability.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company spends steadily about $80,000 per month on Compute Engine, but the mix of machine families and regions changes frequently as teams modernize. It wants a commitment-based discount without locking into specific machine types or regions. What should the architect recommend?
options: Compute flexible committed use discounts (spend-based) covering all eligible compute spend.
Resource-based committed use discounts for specific machine types in a single region.
Sole-tenancy nodes with a one-year commitment for dedicated hardware capacity.
Spot VMs for all workloads with automatic migration to On-Demand when capacity is reclaimed.
questions.correct_rationale: Flexible (spend-based) CUDs apply to eligible compute spend across machine families and regions, fitting a changing mix.
questions.distractor_summary: Resource-based CUDs lock to machine types and regions, sole-tenant nodes cost more, and Spot VMs aren't suitable for steady, interruption-sensitive workloads.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A team runs N2 VMs for about 80% of each month for a project that won't justify a one-year commitment. The finance team asks whether any discount applies without a contract. What should the architect explain?
options: No discounts apply to the instances without a one-year or three-year commitment contract being in place.
Only Spot VMs receive discounts; On-Demand instances are always billed at full price for the whole month.
Sustained use discounts apply automatically to eligible machine types running most of the month.
Discounts require an invoiced billing account with a negotiated enterprise agreement already in place.
questions.correct_rationale: Sustained use discounts are applied automatically for eligible machine series based on usage within the month, requiring no commitment.
questions.distractor_summary: Spot is a separate discount model, and billing account type doesn't determine sustained use eligibility.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A genomics company runs large batch analyses that can be restarted and checkpoint every 10 minutes. Compute is its largest expense. Deadlines are measured in days, not hours. What should the architect recommend to reduce compute cost the most?
options: Three-year committed use discounts applied to the batch compute capacity across all jobs.
Spot VMs in managed instance groups or Batch, which automatically replace preempted capacity during the run.
Memory-optimized machine types to reduce the number of instances needed for each batch job.
Sole-tenant nodes with dedicated physical hardware for the batch analysis workloads.
questions.correct_rationale: Spot VMs offer the largest discounts for fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch work with flexible deadlines, and MIGs or Batch handle preemptions.
questions.distractor_summary: Long commitments fit steady usage rather than bursty batch jobs, and memory-optimized or sole-tenant machines cost more.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A cost review shows that many VMs run at under 10% CPU and memory utilization, and dozens of VMs and persistent disks appear unused. The company wants data-driven recommendations to reduce waste. What should the architect use?
options: Manually inspect each VM's monitoring dashboard and resize the instances by trial and error over several weeks.
Convert all VMs to E2 shared-core machine types regardless of workload requirements.
Buy committed use discounts for the current capacity levels before making any other changes to the fleet.
Active Assist recommendations, including VM rightsizing, idle VM, and idle disk identification.
questions.correct_rationale: Recommender (Active Assist) analyzes utilization to suggest rightsizing and to identify idle resources for removal.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual reviews don't scale, blanket downsizing risks performance, and committing to current oversized capacity locks in waste.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A video platform stores user uploads in Standard class. Analysis shows most videos are viewed heavily in the first 30 days, occasionally for the next year, and almost never afterward, but must be retained indefinitely. What should the architect implement?
options: Lifecycle rules transitioning objects to Nearline at 30 days, Coldline at 90, and Archive at 365.
Store everything in Archive storage class from the start to minimize long-term storage costs over time.
Keep everything in the Standard storage class indefinitely for simplicity and fast access to all videos.
Delete videos older than one year to reduce the storage footprint and the associated storage costs.
questions.correct_rationale: Age-based lifecycle transitions match storage cost to declining access frequency while keeping data retained.
questions.distractor_summary: Archive-first would make frequent early access expensive, Standard forever overpays for cold data, and deletion violates retention.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company's BigQuery on-demand costs have become large and unpredictable as dozens of teams run heavy, steady analytical workloads every day. Finance wants predictable spending and the ability to allocate capacity between teams. What should the architect recommend?
options: Move the analytical workloads to Cloud SQL with read replicas for each team's analytical needs.
Limit each analyst to one query per hour and use query queues to manage overall demand across teams.
Switch to BigQuery editions with capacity pricing and slot reservations assigned per team.
Export tables to CSV files for local analysis on each team's own machines and with their own tools.
questions.correct_rationale: Capacity-based pricing with reservations provides predictable cost and allows allocating slots to different teams, which suits heavy steady workloads.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud SQL isn't an analytics warehouse, query rationing harms productivity, and local exports lose governance and scale.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company processes data in `us-central1` but stores the source data in a bucket in `asia-northeast1`, and it serves large downloads directly from Compute Engine to users worldwide. Network costs are growing rapidly. What should the architect recommend?
options: Upgrade all VMs to larger machine types to handle the network throughput demands.
Co-locate storage and processing in one region and serve downloads through Cloud CDN.
Move all data to a multi-region bucket in the US to reduce inter-region transfer charges.
Switch processing workloads to Spot VMs to reduce the compute costs associated with transfers.
questions.correct_rationale: Keeping data and compute in the same region avoids inter-region transfer charges, and Cloud CDN caching reduces repeated egress from origins.
questions.distractor_summary: Machine size and Spot VMs don't affect network costs, and moving data to a US multi-region doesn't address global download costs by itself.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: A company's development and test environments run 150 Compute Engine VMs 24/7, but developers only work weekdays from 8 AM to 7 PM. The team wants to cut these costs without changing applications. What should the architect recommend?
options: Buy committed use discounts for the development VMs to reduce the hourly compute rate.
Delete development environments at night and recreate them manually each week or month as needed.
Move development VMs to sole-tenant nodes for better isolation and performance guarantees across projects.
Use instance schedules to stop development VMs outside working hours and restart on weekdays.
questions.correct_rationale: Instance schedules automatically stop and start VMs, eliminating compute charges during the roughly two-thirds of the week they aren't used.
questions.distractor_summary: Commitments charge for capacity 24/7, manual recreation is costly in effort, and sole-tenant nodes increase cost.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: An internal tool receives a few hundred requests per day, mostly during business hours. It currently runs on a GKE Standard cluster with three nodes that are almost always idle. Leadership wants to minimize cost while keeping the containerized application. What should the architect recommend?
options: Move the containerized application to Cloud Run with request-based billing and scale-to-zero.
Keep GKE and add a fourth node for additional redundancy and capacity headroom.
Convert the nodes to larger machine types to handle peak traffic more efficiently.
Buy a three-year commitment for the existing node capacity to reduce the overall hourly rate.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Run charges only while handling requests and scales to zero, which suits low-traffic containers.
questions.distractor_summary: More or larger nodes increase cost, and a commitment locks in paying for idle capacity.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution Architecture
questions.question: The CFO asks the architect to justify migrating from an on-premises data center to Google Cloud. The architect's analysis compares only on-premises server hardware costs with the monthly Compute Engine bill, and the CFO calls it incomplete. What should the architect include in a proper total cost of ownership analysis?
options: Include software license costs, facilities overhead, staff time, hardware refresh, and networking in the comparison.
Include only Google Cloud list prices without considering discounts or committed use options.
Facilities, power, cooling, hardware refresh, licensing, labor, and migration vs. cloud costs with discounts.
Include only the cost of the network connection to Google Cloud in the comparison.
questions.correct_rationale: TCO compares all direct and indirect costs over time, including facilities, refresh cycles, licensing, labor, and migration, against cloud costs with discounts and operational changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Considering only hardware, licenses, list prices, or connectivity misses major cost drivers.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A company is building its Google Cloud landing zone for 60 application teams. Requirements: central control of networking, separate production and non-production environments, centralized log retention for audits, and application teams owning their own projects and costs. Which foundation design best fits?
options: One project per team with its own standalone VPC and logs, with no folder hierarchy.
Folders for prod and non-prod, Shared VPC hosts per environment, service projects per team, central logging.
A single project for all teams with IAM separation by labels and naming conventions.
One VPC per application, fully meshed with VPC Network Peering, with centralized logs kept in each project's own sink.
questions.correct_rationale: Environment folders, per-environment Shared VPC hosts, team service projects, and centralized aggregated logging satisfy central control, isolation, team ownership, and audit retention.
questions.distractor_summary: Standalone or peered VPCs fragment network governance, and a single shared project mixes IAM and costs.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A company acquired a startup that has its own Google Cloud organization with 25 projects. The parent company wants to bring the projects under its own organization's policies, billing, and IAM without redeploying workloads. What should the architect recommend?
options: Recreate all resources in new projects under the parent organization from scratch, then delete the old ones.
Grant parent-company admins the Owner role in the startup's organization and keep the organizations separate.
Migrate the startup's projects into a folder in the parent org after reviewing policy differences.
Link the startup's projects to the parent's billing account while keeping IAM and policies separate.
questions.correct_rationale: Projects can be moved between organizations, bringing them under the destination's inherited policies and IAM without redeployment, once the source and destination allow it.
questions.distractor_summary: Rebuilding is costly, separate organizations don't unify governance, and linking billing leaves policies and IAM separate.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: In a shared folder, production and development projects coexist. Security wants external IP addresses to be forbidden only on production resources, but allowed in development, without reorganizing folders. What should the architect use?
options: Resource Manager tags bound to projects with org policy tag-based conditions to enforce per-tag constraints.
Labels on projects with organization policies that can read and evaluate label values at enforcement time.
Separate billing accounts for production to prevent external IP charges from non-production workloads.
Firewall rules that block external traffic in production, applied at the VPC level for each subnet.
questions.correct_rationale: Organization policies support conditions based on tags, allowing different enforcement for tagged resources in the same folder.
questions.distractor_summary: Labels can't be used in organization policy conditions, billing accounts don't affect policy, and firewall rules don't prevent external IP assignment.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A company is preparing a global product launch across 40 projects and several regions. In past launches, teams hit regional CPU and IP address quotas unexpectedly. The architect wants proactive, automated quota management. What should the architect recommend?
options: Ask each team to check quotas manually in the console one day before the scheduled launch date of the event.
Request the maximum possible quota in every region for every project well before the scheduled launch date.
Consolidate all workloads into one project to share a single set of regional quota limits.
Forecast capacity per project and region, manage quotas via the Cloud Quotas API, and alert on thresholds.
questions.correct_rationale: Capacity forecasting combined with programmatic quota management and usage alerts prevents launch-day quota failures.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual checks are late and error-prone, blanket maximum requests may be denied and hide real needs, and one project concentrates quota limits and blast radius.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A security team wants to be notified within minutes whenever anyone in the organization creates or modifies a Cloud Storage bucket, so that an automated function can check whether it's publicly accessible and remediate it. What should the architect design?
options: A daily Cloud Scheduler job that lists all buckets and checks their IAM configuration for public access.
A Cloud Asset Inventory real-time feed for bucket changes, publishing to Pub/Sub to trigger remediation.
Billing export alerts that fire when Cloud Storage costs change unexpectedly across the organization.
Weekly Security Command Center reports listing buckets with public access or weak IAM bindings.
questions.correct_rationale: Asset Inventory feeds push resource changes to Pub/Sub in near real time, which can trigger automated checks and remediation.
questions.distractor_summary: Daily listing and weekly reports are too slow, and billing data doesn't reflect configuration changes.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: Auditors require that all audit logs across 300 projects be retained for five years in one place that project owners can't alter, while application teams should still be able to view logs for their own projects. What should the architect design?
options: An organization-level aggregated sink routing audit logs to a locked central log bucket with five-year retention, plus log views for each team's own projects.
Increase retention on each project's _Default log bucket to five years, with log bucket locking enabled on it.
Export logs from each project to that project's own BigQuery dataset, with a five-year table expiration set.
Grant auditors the Logging Admin role on every project so that they can access, view, and export audit logs.
questions.correct_rationale: Aggregated sinks centralize logs from all projects into a controlled bucket where retention can be locked, and log views provide scoped access for teams. Per-project locked buckets still leave logs distributed across 300 projects rather than in one place.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-project locked buckets don't satisfy the single-location requirement; per-project BigQuery exports aren't centralized; Logging Admin on every project doesn't centralize retention.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: Finance requires every production resource to carry `cost-center` and `owner` labels for chargeback. Most infrastructure is deployed with Terraform, and teams frequently forget labels. The architect wants to prevent unlabeled resources from being deployed rather than find them later. What should the architect recommend?
options: A monthly script that emails owners of unlabeled resources with a summary report attached.
Budget alerts per project that fire when costs exceed expected thresholds for unlabeled resources.
Policy-as-code checks in the Terraform CI pipeline that fail plans missing required labels.
Grant the finance team Editor role on all projects so they can add labels to existing resources.
questions.correct_rationale: Validating Terraform plans against policies in CI blocks non-compliant changes before deployment, and module defaults reduce mistakes.
questions.distractor_summary: Monthly scripts and budgets detect problems after the fact, and giving finance Editor is excessive and reactive.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: Security wants to require that every new GKE cluster in the organization has Workload Identity Federation enabled and private nodes, blocking non-compliant cluster creation. No predefined organization policy constraint covers both settings. What should the architect use?
options: A Cloud Monitoring alert that fires whenever a new GKE cluster is created in any project of the organization.
An IAM deny policy on the container.clusters.create permission applied across all projects in the organization.
Firewall policies on the GKE node subnets to restrict network access from clusters that are non-compliant.
Custom organization policy constraints for GKE clusters with CEL conditions, enforced at the org level.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom organization policy constraints can evaluate resource fields on create and update, blocking clusters that don't meet requirements.
questions.distractor_summary: Alerts are reactive, a blanket deny prevents all cluster creation, and firewall policies don't validate cluster configuration.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A company with one billing account and 150 projects needs monthly chargeback reports by business unit and application, including shared costs such as networking. Business units want self-service dashboards. What should the architect design?
options: A separate billing account for each application, with consistent labels and Looker Studio dashboards per business unit.
Labels and project metadata for business unit and application, billing export to BigQuery, and Looker dashboards.
Cloud Billing reports in the console, filtered by project labels, then downloaded manually each month by the finance team.
PDF invoices emailed to each business unit at the end of every billing cycle, with spreadsheets attached for each project.
questions.correct_rationale: Labels plus detailed billing export in BigQuery enable flexible allocation, including shared costs, and dashboards provide self-service.
questions.distractor_summary: Many billing accounts complicate governance and discounts, console reports lack custom allocation logic, and invoices aren't broken down by application.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A central network team must control IP address allocation, firewall policies, and hybrid connectivity, while 30 application teams deploy resources independently in their own projects and pay for them. What networking model should the architect choose?
options: Shared VPC, with the network team owning host projects and application teams as service projects.
A standalone VPC per team connected through VPC Network Peering with shared route tables.
One project containing all resources, with IAM roles separating the network and application teams.
Separate VPCs per team connected through HA VPN tunnels that are managed by the central network team.
questions.correct_rationale: Shared VPC centralizes network administration in host projects while resources and costs stay in team service projects.
questions.distractor_summary: Peered or VPN-connected VPCs distribute network control, and a single project mixes ownership and billing.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A company wants all infrastructure changes to be reviewed and auditable. Engineers should propose changes through pull requests, see the proposed changes before approval, and never apply changes from their laptops. What should the architect design?
options: Engineers run terraform apply locally after getting peer review approval in the team chat channel.
A nightly CI job that applies whatever is in the main branch without any manual review step.
A CI/CD pipeline that runs terraform plan on PRs and terraform apply on merge with a dedicated SA.
Console changes with screenshots attached to change tickets reviewed by the change advisory board.
questions.correct_rationale: Plan-on-PR and apply-on-merge with a dedicated pipeline identity provides review, auditability, and consistent execution.
questions.distractor_summary: Local applies bypass controls, unreviewed nightly applies are risky, and console changes aren't reproducible.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A team manages development, staging, and production with Terraform in a single state file. A mistake in a development change recently caused Terraform to plan the destruction of production resources. How should the architect restructure state management?
options: Keep one state file but review plans more carefully before applying any infrastructure changes.
Store the state file in Git alongside the Terraform configuration for full version history and team review.
Use local state files per engineer with manual coordination to avoid conflicting changes.
Separate state per environment in Cloud Storage backends with versioning, locking, and scoped pipelines.
questions.correct_rationale: Separating state and credentials per environment limits the blast radius, and remote backends provide locking and recovery.
questions.distractor_summary: A single state keeps environments coupled, Git isn't a safe state backend, and local state prevents collaboration.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: Security wants Terraform changes to be checked against organization rules, such as allowed regions, required CMEK, and no public buckets, before changes reach production, so that violations are caught in the pipeline rather than after deployment. What should the architect add?
options: Manual security review of every pull request by a member of the security team.
Policy validation of Terraform plans in CI that fails the build on any rule violations.
Security Command Center scans after deployment with alerts to the security team.
A Cloud Monitoring dashboard showing resource counts and configuration changes over time.
questions.correct_rationale: Policy-as-code in CI evaluates planned changes against rules and blocks violations before deployment.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual reviews are inconsistent, post-deployment scans are detective rather than preventive, and dashboards don't validate configuration.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A company's VMs are patched and configured manually after deployment, leading to configuration drift and inconsistent behavior across instances. The architect wants every instance to be identical and updates to be predictable and reversible. What should the architect recommend?
options: Build versioned machine images through an automated pipeline and roll out using rolling updates.
Use SSH scripts to patch each VM nightly and record any configuration changes in a shared spreadsheet.
Allow teams to log in and fix configuration problems individually on their own running instances.
Take snapshots of each VM weekly and restore them from the snapshot if configuration drift is detected.
questions.correct_rationale: Immutable infrastructure with baked images and rolling updates ensures consistency and allows rollback to previous templates.
questions.distractor_summary: SSH patching and manual fixes cause drift, and snapshots back up data rather than preventing inconsistency.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A team uses Terraform to create Cloud SQL users and passes the database passwords as Terraform variables. A security review notes that the passwords are visible in the Terraform state file. What should the architect recommend?
options: Encrypt the Terraform variables file with a password before committing it to the shared Git repository.
Store the Terraform state file on an engineer's laptop instead of in shared cloud storage.
Use Terraform to create Secret Manager resources, but set values outside Terraform to keep them out of state.
Disable state locking to prevent concurrent access issues in the shared state file.
questions.correct_rationale: Terraform stores resource attributes, including secret values, in state, so keeping secret material out of Terraform and in Secret Manager reduces exposure.
questions.distractor_summary: Encrypting a variables file doesn't protect state, local state increases risk, and locking is unrelated.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A company deploys containerized services to Cloud Run and GKE in development, staging, and production. It wants a managed pipeline that promotes the same release artifact through environments, requires approval before production, supports canary rollouts, and records release history. What should the architect use?
options: Separate Cloud Build triggers that rebuild container images independently for each target environment in the pipeline.
Manual kubectl and gcloud commands executed by engineers for each environment's deployment steps and approvals.
Cloud Scheduler jobs that deploy new versions to each environment on a nightly schedule.
Cloud Deploy delivery pipelines with per-environment targets, production approvals, and canary strategies.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Deploy promotes a single release through ordered targets with approvals, canary strategies, and history.
questions.distractor_summary: Rebuilding per environment breaks artifact consistency, manual commands aren't auditable, and scheduled deploys don't provide controlled promotion.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: Application teams request new projects about 20 times a month. Each project must have standard APIs enabled, a budget, default labels, Shared VPC attachment, log sinks, and baseline IAM. Manual setup takes days and is inconsistent. What should the architect recommend?
options: A document of manual setup steps that each team follows whenever it creates new projects by hand in the console.
A project factory: a Terraform module invoked from a request pipeline with baseline configuration.
Grant every team the Project Creator role and let them configure projects entirely on their own without guardrails.
Reuse one shared project for all new applications with IAM separation by labels and per-team service accounts.
questions.correct_rationale: A project factory automates consistent project creation with baseline configuration and reduces lead time.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual steps and self-service without guardrails produce inconsistency, and reusing one project loses isolation.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A Terraform change applied through CI modified a load balancer configuration and caused an outage. The team needs a reliable way to return to the last known good infrastructure configuration. What should the architect put in place?
options: Version-controlled Terraform code with pinned modules, revertible commits, and state bucket versioning.
Console edits to manually reverse the change and restore the previous load balancer configuration from memory.
Delete the load balancer and recreate it manually, using the previous settings as a reference guide document.
Disable Terraform management for the load balancer permanently and manage it entirely by hand from then on.
questions.correct_rationale: Reverting code and reapplying through the pipeline restores a known configuration reproducibly, and state versioning helps recover from state issues.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual console fixes create drift, manual recreation risks more downtime, and abandoning IaC removes control.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: Production infrastructure is managed by Terraform, but engineers occasionally change settings in the console during incidents, and those changes are overwritten or cause drift. The architect wants to prevent routine console changes while still allowing emergencies. What should the architect recommend?
options: Give all engineers the Owner role and ask them to document any console changes they make.
Disable Cloud Audit Logs to reduce noise and prevent drift detection from triggering alerts.
Grant write access only to the CI/CD service account; engineers get read-only and break-glass access.
Run terraform apply every five minutes to overwrite any manual console changes made during incidents.
questions.correct_rationale: Limiting write access to the pipeline identity prevents drift, while break-glass access (for example, through Privileged Access Manager) covers emergencies with auditing.
questions.distractor_summary: Broad Owner access permits drift, disabling audit logs removes accountability, and constant reapplication can override emergency fixes unpredictably.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.question: A platform team already uses a GitOps workflow for Kubernetes applications across GKE clusters. It wants to manage Google Cloud resources such as Pub/Sub topics, Cloud SQL instances, and IAM bindings through the same Git repositories and reconciliation model. What should the architect recommend?
options: Terraform run manually by the platform team whenever Google Cloud resources need to be changed or updated.
gcloud scripts triggered by Git commits to provision and update cloud resources in each project.
Deployment Manager templates stored in the Git repository alongside Kubernetes manifests.
Config Connector for Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources, synced from Git.
questions.correct_rationale: Config Connector represents Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes objects, and Config Sync continuously reconciles them from Git, extending the existing GitOps model.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual Terraform and scripts don't provide continuous reconciliation, and Deployment Manager isn't part of the Kubernetes workflow.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A company operates GKE clusters for development, staging, and production. It wants new Kubernetes versions to reach staging before production, production upgrades to be conservative, and node upgrades in production to allow quick rollback if workloads misbehave. What should the architect recommend?
options: Pin all clusters to one Kubernetes version and disable automatic upgrades entirely.
Enroll staging in the Regular release channel and production in Stable, with blue-green upgrades.
Enroll all clusters in the Rapid release channel to get the latest Kubernetes features as soon as possible.
Upgrade production manually first, then staging, to test the new version on live traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: Release channels stage versions so staging sees them earlier than production, and blue-green node upgrades keep the old node pool available for rollback.
questions.distractor_summary: Disabling upgrades leads to unsupported versions, Rapid is risky for production, and upgrading production first inverts safe practice.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: An online retailer's Cloud SQL instance occasionally restarts for maintenance during peak shopping hours. The retailer also wants no maintenance at all during the November holiday season. What should the architect configure?
options: A maintenance window during low-traffic hours and a deny period covering the holiday season.
Disable Cloud SQL maintenance permanently to prevent any restarts during peak shopping periods.
Move the database to a Compute Engine VM so the team can control patching schedules manually.
Create read replicas to absorb restarts and redirect read traffic during maintenance events.
questions.correct_rationale: Maintenance windows control when updates occur, and deny periods block maintenance during critical periods.
questions.distractor_summary: Maintenance can't be disabled indefinitely, self-managing adds operations burden, and read replicas don't serve writes during primary maintenance.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A media company's Spanner instance handles traffic that varies fivefold between daytime and night. The team currently provisions for peak capacity around the clock and wants to reduce cost without manual intervention while maintaining performance. What should the architect recommend?
options: Reduce the Spanner instance to night-time capacity permanently to save on idle costs.
Migrate the workload to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with read replicas for daytime traffic.
Enable Spanner's managed autoscaler with min/max limits and a target CPU utilization.
Create a second Spanner instance for daytime traffic and shut down the first at night.
questions.correct_rationale: Spanner's managed autoscaler adjusts compute capacity within limits based on utilization, reducing cost during quiet periods.
questions.distractor_summary: Permanent reduction harms daytime performance, Cloud SQL lacks Spanner's scale characteristics, and a second instance adds complexity without solving scaling.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A 50 TB BigQuery events table is queried mostly by date range and frequently filtered by `customer_id`. Query costs are high, and data older than two years must be deleted automatically. What should the architect recommend?
options: Split the table into one table per customer to reduce the scan size for each query.
Export old data to CSV files and delete it manually on a quarterly schedule.
Create materialized views for every customer to precompute their common query results.
Partition by event date with a two-year expiration, and cluster by customer_id.
questions.correct_rationale: Date partitioning limits bytes scanned for date-range queries, partition expiration removes old data automatically, and clustering by `customer_id` reduces scanned data within partitions.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-customer tables are hard to manage, manual exports are error-prone, and per-customer materialized views don't scale.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A law firm stores case documents in Cloud Storage with a lifecycle rule that deletes objects after seven years. When litigation begins on a case, the related documents must be preserved indefinitely until the hold is released, regardless of the lifecycle rule. What should the architect recommend?
