options: Disable the lifecycle deletion rule for the entire bucket during the ongoing litigation period.
Place object holds on the affected objects to prevent deletion until the hold is released.
Copy the documents to a separate bucket manually and exclude it from lifecycle rules.
Change the storage class to Archive so the lifecycle rule doesn't apply to those objects.
questions.correct_rationale: Object holds prevent deletion or replacement of specific objects until the hold is removed, overriding lifecycle deletion.
questions.distractor_summary: Disabling the rule affects all objects, manual copies are error-prone, and storage class doesn't prevent deletion.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A SaaS company lets 5,000 customers use their own custom domains for the company's application behind a global external Application Load Balancer. It needs Google-managed certificates for each domain and expects the number of domains to keep growing. What should the architect recommend?
options: Certificate Manager with certificate maps and entries for each customer domain on the target proxy.
Classic SSL certificates attached directly to the load balancer's target proxy for each customer domain.
One self-managed wildcard certificate covering all of the customer domains behind the load balancer.
A separate load balancer with its own Google-managed certificate for each of the 5,000 customer domains.
questions.correct_rationale: Certificate Manager scales to many certificates through certificate maps and supports Google-managed certificates for customer domains.
questions.distractor_summary: Classic target proxy certificates have low limits, a wildcard can't cover domains the company doesn't own, and per-customer load balancers are costly.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A company runs a stateful message broker cluster on Compute Engine VMs. Each VM needs to keep its persistent data disk, instance name, and internal IP address when it's recreated during autohealing or updates. The team wants managed instance group features such as autohealing and rolling updates. What should the architect use?
options: Unmanaged instance groups with manual scripts to preserve disk and IP configuration.
A stateless regional managed instance group with local SSDs for persistent data storage on each VM.
A stateful managed instance group with stateful policies that preserve disks, instance names, and internal IPs.
GKE Autopilot Deployments with persistent volumes for the message broker data.
questions.correct_rationale: Stateful MIGs preserve per-instance state such as disks, names, and IPs while providing autohealing and updates.
questions.distractor_summary: Unmanaged groups lack these features, stateless MIGs discard instance state, and Deployments don't preserve per-Pod identity.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A retailer runs its annual sales event and needs 400 A2 GPU VMs in `us-central1` for real-time recommendations during a two-week window. In previous years, VM creation failed because capacity wasn't available in the zone. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use Spot VMs for the event to take advantage of spare capacity at a much lower price per hour.
Increase the GPU quota in us-central1 to allow more concurrent VMs during the two-week sales event.
Deploy across random regions during the event to find available GPU capacity.
Create Compute Engine reservations for the required machine types and zones ahead of time.
questions.correct_rationale: Reservations guarantee capacity for specific machine types in a zone, protecting critical events from stockouts.
questions.distractor_summary: Spot VMs can be preempted, quota doesn't guarantee available capacity, and random placement adds latency and complexity.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A company stores 800 TB of rarely changed BigQuery data. The data compresses very well, and storage costs are a large share of the BigQuery bill. What should the architect evaluate?
options: Moving all the data to Cloud SQL to take advantage of different storage pricing tiers.
Switching datasets to physical (compressed) storage billing after estimating the savings.
Duplicating tables into a second dataset to test whether compression improves performance.
Exporting data to Cloud Storage Standard class and querying it through BigQuery external tables.
questions.correct_rationale: Physical storage billing charges for compressed bytes, which can significantly reduce costs for highly compressible data, and long-term pricing already applies to tables unmodified for 90 days.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud SQL isn't suited to this scale, duplication increases cost, and exporting loses query performance.

questions.domain: 2. Managing and Provisioning a Solution Infrastructure
questions.subdomain: 2.3 Managing compute, storage, data, and networking
questions.question: A company migrated its Hadoop workloads to a long-running Dataproc cluster that's busy two hours a night and idle the rest of the day, with data stored in HDFS on the cluster. Costs are high, and losing the cluster would lose data. What should the architect recommend?
options: Store data in Cloud Storage and use ephemeral Dataproc clusters that are deleted after jobs finish.
Double the cluster size to finish jobs faster, but keep the cluster running around the clock all week.
Keep the cluster running all week and buy committed use discounts to reduce the hourly compute rates.
Move HDFS data to local SSDs on the cluster nodes for faster access during job execution runs each night.
questions.correct_rationale: Separating storage in Cloud Storage from ephemeral compute removes idle costs and protects data from cluster loss.
questions.distractor_summary: A larger always-on cluster increases cost, commitments lock in idle spend, and local SSDs increase the risk of data loss.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: An insurance company requires separation of duties in production: developers must be able to deploy and operate applications but must not be able to change IAM policies, while the security team must manage IAM but must not be able to deploy or modify workloads. Currently everyone has the Editor or Owner role. What should the architect recommend?
options: Keep the Owner role for everyone, but review the audit logs weekly for unauthorized changes made by users.
Give developers the Editor role and the security team the Owner role on all of the projects in the folder.
Remove basic roles; give developers deployment roles and security IAM admin roles separately.
Create one custom role combining deployment and IAM permissions for both groups to share equally.
questions.correct_rationale: Separation of duties requires distinct role sets, with developers holding service-specific roles and security holding IAM administration without workload access.
questions.distractor_summary: Owner lets anyone do both, Editor is still overly broad, and a combined custom role defeats the separation.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: During a security review of a new Google Cloud organization, an auditor finds that the Cloud Identity super admin role is assigned to three engineers' everyday accounts, which they use for daily work and email. What should the architect recommend?
options: Create dedicated super admin accounts with hardware keys, used only for rare admin tasks.
Remove all super admin accounts from the organization and rely on folder-level admin roles.
Share one super admin password among the engineers with a password rotation schedule.
Grant the super admin role to all engineers so no one person is a single point of failure.
questions.correct_rationale: Google recommends dedicated, strongly protected super admin accounts reserved for rare tasks, reducing exposure from daily activities like email.
questions.distractor_summary: An organization needs at least one super admin, shared passwords remove accountability, and granting it to everyone increases risk.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: After a project with critical data was deleted by a project owner, security wants to guarantee that only members of a platform team can delete projects anywhere in the organization, regardless of any role grants. What should the architect implement?
options: Remove the Owner role from all users across the organization and audit the existing role bindings regularly.
Place liens on every existing project manually to prevent deletion by non-platform users.
Create an organization policy that disables project deletion for all principals in the organization.
An IAM deny policy at the org level denying project deletion, with the platform team excepted.
questions.correct_rationale: Deny policies override allow grants and can include exceptions, enforcing the rule across all current and future projects.
questions.distractor_summary: Removing Owner doesn't cover other roles with delete permissions, liens must be added per project and don't cover new ones automatically, and no organization policy constraint blocks project deletion this way.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A team built a custom role with a precise list of permissions for its operators. After a Google Cloud service introduced a new feature, operators can't use it, while users with the equivalent predefined role can. What explains this, and what should the architect recommend?
options: Custom roles expire after one year and must be recreated with the updated permission list included.
Custom roles don't receive new permissions automatically; review and update when services change.
Predefined roles have higher priority than custom roles when both are assigned to a user.
The operators need the Owner role to access new features introduced by Google Cloud services.
questions.correct_rationale: Google updates predefined roles with new permissions, but custom roles contain only the permissions you list, so they require ongoing maintenance.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom roles don't expire, roles don't have priority ordering, and Owner is excessive.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company uses Workload Identity Federation so GitHub Actions can impersonate a production deployment service account. Security discovers that any workflow in any repository of the company's GitHub organization could impersonate it. Only workflows running on the `main` branch of the `infra-prod` repository should be allowed. What should the architect change?
options: Rotate the service account's keys and distribute the new keys to the GitHub workflows.
Move the service account to a different project that only the infra-prod team can access directly.
Add attribute conditions on the workload identity provider restricting repo and ref claims.
Require all GitHub users in the organization to enable MFA on their accounts.
questions.correct_rationale: Attribute conditions and principal-set bindings restrict which external identities can exchange tokens or impersonate the service account, based on claims like repository and ref.
questions.distractor_summary: Federation uses no keys, moving projects doesn't limit federation, and user MFA doesn't restrict which workflows can impersonate.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company wants the compliance team to have read access to every project tagged `data-classification=restricted` across the organization, including projects created in the future, without maintaining bindings per project. What should the architect implement?
options: A conditional IAM binding at the org level matching resources with the data-classification tag.
Grant the compliance team the Viewer role on each restricted project manually as they're created.
Use resource labels in the IAM condition to match projects tagged data-classification=restricted.
Create a separate organization for restricted projects and grant compliance access there.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM Conditions can check tags attached to resources, so a single organization-level binding applies to every tagged project, including new ones.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual bindings don't scale, labels can't be used in IAM conditions, and a separate organization fragments governance.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A service account key for a production data pipeline was found in a public code repository. What sequence of actions should the architect recommend?
options: Delete the public repository and continue using the exposed key until the next scheduled rotation cycle.
Delete the service account immediately, without first investigating what the exposed key had been used for.
Rotate the key next quarter and monitor for any unauthorized use of the exposed key in the meantime, as needed.
Disable the exposed key, audit usage logs, remediate changes, move to keyless auth, block key creation.
questions.correct_rationale: Incident response should revoke the credential, investigate its use, remediate, and prevent recurrence with keyless authentication and policy.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting the repo doesn't revoke the key, deleting the account without investigation loses context and breaks the pipeline, and delayed rotation leaves the key usable.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company enforces domain restricted sharing so IAM can only grant roles to its own Cloud Identity principals. A joint project with a partner requires granting the partner's Google Workspace users access to one shared project. What should the architect do?
options: Disable domain restricted sharing across the organization to allow external partner access.
Override the iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains policy on the shared project to include the partner.
Create Cloud Identity accounts in the company domain for every partner user who needs access.
Share service account keys with the partner so they can authenticate to the shared project.
questions.correct_rationale: The constraint can be overridden at the project level to add the partner's customer ID, allowing a scoped exception.
questions.distractor_summary: Disabling it globally weakens security, duplicate accounts complicate identity management, and sharing keys is insecure.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: Before a regulatory audit, the security team must determine which principals, including groups, service accounts, and inherited grants, can read a sensitive BigQuery dataset across the organization. What should the architect use?
options: Read the dataset's IAM policy in the console to see the directly attached role bindings.
VPC Flow Logs to see which principals have been accessing the BigQuery dataset recently.
Policy Analyzer to analyze who has access, including inherited and group-expanded bindings.
The Billing export to identify which principals have been incurring charges on the dataset.
questions.correct_rationale: Policy Analyzer evaluates IAM across the hierarchy, expanding groups and inherited bindings, to answer who can access a resource.
questions.distractor_summary: The dataset policy alone misses inherited grants, and flow logs and billing data don't describe permissions.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company uses CMEK for Cloud Storage and wants keys rotated every 90 days. A team member asks whether existing objects will be re-encrypted with the new key version and whether old data will still be readable. What should the architect explain?
options: Configure automatic key rotation; new versions encrypt new data, old versions decrypt existing data.
Key rotation re-encrypts all existing objects immediately with the new primary key version automatically.
Rotation immediately disables old key versions, making all objects encrypted with them unreadable afterward.
Key rotation isn't supported for customer-managed encryption keys in Cloud KMS.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud KMS rotation creates new primary versions for new encryption while prior versions remain available for decryption, and data is re-encrypted only when rewritten.
questions.distractor_summary: Rotation doesn't bulk re-encrypt or disable old versions, and it's fully supported.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A SaaS company stores data for many customers in shared Cloud Storage buckets and BigQuery datasets. Contracts require that when a customer leaves, all of their data become unrecoverable quickly, including backups. What design should the architect recommend?
options: Delete the customer's rows and objects and wait for all backups to expire naturally.
Use one CMEK key for all customers and manage access through IAM policies per customer.
Rely on default Google encryption and use object lifecycle rules to delete customer data.
Encrypt each customer's data with a dedicated CMEK key and destroy it on offboarding.
questions.correct_rationale: Per-customer keys make data unreadable everywhere, including backups, once the key is destroyed.
questions.distractor_summary: Waiting for backups to expire is slow, a shared key can't be destroyed for one customer, and default encryption doesn't give per-customer control.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A payment processor must use encryption keys stored in hardware security modules validated to FIPS 140-2 Level 3, managed within Google Cloud, to protect data in Cloud SQL and Cloud Storage. What should the architect recommend?
options: Cloud KMS software keys with automatic rotation enabled every 90 days.
Cloud KMS keys with the HSM protection level (Cloud HSM) used as CMEK.
Customer-supplied encryption keys generated and managed outside of Google Cloud.
Default Google encryption with no customer-managed key configuration required.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud HSM keys are stored in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSMs and can be used as CMEK for supported services.
questions.distractor_summary: Software keys don't meet the HSM requirement, CSEK isn't supported by all services and isn't HSM-backed by Google, and default encryption doesn't give customer control.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A BigQuery customer table contains email addresses and phone numbers. Marketing analysts need all columns except that PII columns must show masked values, while the privacy team sees clear values. The rules must apply wherever the columns are queried. What should the architect implement?
options: Create separate copies of the table for each group, with the PII columns masked or removed entirely.
Encrypt the PII columns with a shared encryption key and give the decryption key only to the privacy team.
Apply policy tags with dynamic data masking rules for analysts and Fine-Grained Reader for privacy.
Use authorized views that exclude the PII columns entirely for the marketing analyst group members only.
questions.correct_rationale: Policy tags enforce column-level access, and dynamic data masking returns masked values to authorized users without copies.
questions.distractor_summary: Table copies drift and cost more, shared-key encryption complicates access management, and views that drop columns don't provide masked values.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A global sales table in BigQuery is used by regional managers. Each manager must see only rows for their own region, and new rows must be filtered automatically without maintaining separate tables. What should the architect implement?
options: Row-level access policies on the table that filter rows by region for each regional group.
One table per region with separate IAM bindings for each regional manager's group of users.
Column-level security with policy tags to restrict which columns each regional manager can view.
VPC Service Controls per region to restrict API access to the sales data by geographic location.
questions.correct_rationale: Row-level security policies filter rows based on the querying principal, applying to all current and future rows.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-region tables add maintenance, column-level security controls columns rather than rows, and VPC Service Controls protects API access rather than filtering rows.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A regulator requires that all service-to-service communication between a bank's microservices on GKE be encrypted and mutually authenticated at the application layer, with evidence of which services communicate. What should the architect recommend?
options: Rely on Google's default encryption at the physical network layer for all inter-service traffic.
Use HA VPN tunnels between Kubernetes namespaces to encrypt service-to-service communication.
Enable CMEK on the GKE boot disks to encrypt data at rest on the cluster nodes.
Deploy Cloud Service Mesh with strict mTLS and authorization policies for service evidence.
questions.correct_rationale: A service mesh provides mutually authenticated, encrypted connections between services with identity-based policies and telemetry.
questions.distractor_summary: Default infrastructure encryption doesn't provide application-layer mutual authentication, VPN doesn't operate between namespaces, and CMEK protects data at rest.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A manufacturer needs to issue and manage private TLS certificates for 50,000 IoT devices and internal services, with automated issuance, revocation, and a CA hierarchy whose root keys are HSM-protected. It doesn't want to run its own PKI servers. What should the architect recommend?
options: Self-signed certificates generated and managed independently on each IoT device in the field.
Certificate Authority Service with a root and subordinate CA pool backed by Cloud HSM keys.
Certificate Manager for all device certificates with Google-managed issuance and renewal.
Public certificates from a commercial CA for every IoT device and internal service endpoint.
questions.correct_rationale: Certificate Authority Service provides a managed private PKI with HSM-backed keys, CA hierarchies, and APIs for issuance and revocation at scale.
questions.distractor_summary: Self-signed certificates lack central trust and revocation, Certificate Manager is for load balancer certificates, and public certificates for private devices are costly and unnecessary.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: Three hospitals want to jointly train a model on their combined patient data. None may see the others' raw data, and the processing environment must prove to each hospital that only the approved workload can decrypt and use the data. What should the architect recommend?
options: Copy all hospital data into a shared BigQuery dataset with IAM restrictions applied per hospital team.
Use VPC Service Controls perimeters around a shared project to prevent data exfiltration.
Confidential Space with an attested workload so each party releases keys only to the approved code.
Encrypt data with CMEK and share the decryption key among the three hospital teams.
questions.correct_rationale: Confidential Space uses attestation so data owners grant key access only to a verified workload, enabling multi-party computation without exposing raw data to other parties or operators.
questions.distractor_summary: Shared datasets and shared keys expose data to participants, and VPC Service Controls doesn't provide workload attestation.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company has thousands of BigQuery tables across hundreds of projects, and nobody knows where sensitive data such as national IDs and health information resides. The data governance team needs an organization-wide inventory of sensitive data with ongoing updates. What should the architect recommend?
options: Enable Sensitive Data Protection discovery at the org level to profile BigQuery data continuously.
Ask each team to document their tables and submit an inventory spreadsheet to the governance team.
Run one-time manual queries searching for common PII patterns across all projects and tables.
Use Cloud Asset Inventory to classify table contents and generate a sensitive data report.
questions.correct_rationale: Sensitive Data Protection discovery continuously profiles data across the organization and identifies sensitive information types and risk.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual documentation and one-time queries are incomplete, and Asset Inventory tracks resource metadata rather than content.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company wants to prevent exfiltration of data from its BigQuery and Cloud Storage projects to projects outside the company, even by insiders with valid credentials. Data engineers must still reach the console from corporate offices. What should the architect design?
options: Firewall rules blocking internet egress from all VMs in the data processing projects.
IAM deny policies preventing all external users from accessing BigQuery and Cloud Storage data.
Cloud Armor policies applied to BigQuery and Cloud Storage API endpoints.
A VPC Service Controls perimeter with access levels for corporate IPs and approved identities.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC Service Controls blocks API-level data movement across the perimeter, including by authorized insiders, and access levels permit approved contexts like corporate networks.
questions.distractor_summary: Firewall rules don't control Google API data movement, deny policies can't prevent copies to external projects by permitted users, and Cloud Armor doesn't front these APIs.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company plans to enforce a VPC Service Controls perimeter around 40 existing projects with many integrations. The security team worries that enforcement might break production pipelines in ways it can't predict. What should the architect recommend?
options: Enforce the perimeter immediately and fix any pipeline failures as they're reported by teams.
Configure the perimeter in dry-run mode, analyze violation logs, add rules, then enforce it.
Skip VPC Service Controls entirely and rely on IAM policies alone to prevent data exfiltration.
Enforce the perimeter on one project per week without monitoring for service disruptions in pipelines.
questions.correct_rationale: Dry-run mode logs what would be blocked without enforcing, letting teams build the needed rules before enforcement.
questions.distractor_summary: Immediate enforcement risks outages, IAM alone doesn't prevent exfiltration, and gradual rollout without monitoring still causes surprises.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: An analytics project inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter must load files from a partner's Cloud Storage bucket in a project outside the perimeter using a specific service account. All other access across the perimeter must remain blocked. What should the architect configure?
options: Remove the analytics project from the perimeter so it can access the partner's bucket freely.
Add the partner's project to the company's VPC Service Controls perimeter as an exception.
An egress rule allowing that service account to call Cloud Storage read on the partner's project.
A firewall rule allowing traffic to the partner's bucket from the analytics subnets and routes.
questions.correct_rationale: Egress rules allow narrowly scoped access from inside the perimeter to external resources for specific identities, services, and methods.
questions.distractor_summary: Removing the project or adding a third party's project weakens the perimeter, and firewall rules don't govern API access.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A public e-commerce website behind a global external Application Load Balancer is receiving SQL injection attempts and large L7 floods during sales events. The company needs WAF protection and DDoS mitigation at Google's edge. What should the architect recommend?
options: Cloud Armor security policies with WAF rules, rate limiting, and Adaptive Protection on the backend.
VPC firewall rules blocking suspicious IP addresses on the backend VMs serving the website traffic to users.
Cloud NGFW Enterprise on the web servers' subnets to inspect and block malicious L7 traffic and exploits.
Identity-Aware Proxy on the public website to authenticate users before they can browse.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Armor provides edge WAF rules, rate limiting, and ML-based L7 DDoS detection for load balancer backends.
questions.distractor_summary: VPC firewall rules and NGFW act after traffic reaches the VPC, and IAP requires user authentication, which isn't suitable for public shoppers.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: Administrators currently SSH into production VMs through bastion hosts with public IP addresses. Security wants to eliminate public IPs on all VMs, require identity-based and audited administrative access, and prevent anyone from adding public IPs again. What should the architect recommend?
options: Keep the bastion hosts but restrict SSH access to known office IP address ranges only, with logging.
Use Cloud VPN tunnels for every administrator's laptop to reach production VMs securely and privately.
Assign public IPs to VMs only during scheduled maintenance windows and remove them again after the work.
Use IAP TCP forwarding for SSH/RDP, remove external IPs and bastions, enforce the org policy.
questions.correct_rationale: IAP TCP forwarding provides identity-aware, audited access without public IPs, and the organization policy prevents reintroducing them.
questions.distractor_summary: Bastions with public IPs keep exposure, per-laptop VPN adds complexity, and temporary public IPs still create windows of exposure.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A healthcare company must detect and block known exploits and malware in east-west traffic between application tiers inside its VPC, using a Google-managed service rather than third-party appliances. What should the architect recommend?
options: Cloud Armor security policies applied to internal load balancer traffic between application tiers in the VPC.
Cloud NGFW Enterprise with intrusion prevention profiles applied through network firewall policies.
VPC Flow Logs with Cloud Monitoring alerting on suspicious traffic patterns between the application tiers.
Cloud IDS for detection of threats in east-west traffic between application tiers, with alerts in Logging.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud NGFW Enterprise inspects traffic in-line and can block threats between workloads.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Armor protects traffic at load balancers, flow logs don't inspect payloads, and Cloud IDS detects but doesn't block.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company wants the central security team to enforce baseline firewall rules across all VPCs, such as blocking known-bad ranges and allowing health checks, while delegating application-specific rules to each business unit's network team for its own folder. What should the architect design?
options: A single VPC firewall rule set copied into every VPC by the central security team.
Organization policies restricting which firewall rules can be created in each project.
Hierarchical firewall policies at the org level for baseline, folder-level for business units.
Cloud Armor edge policies for internal traffic between application tiers in each VPC.
questions.correct_rationale: Hierarchical policies let the organization enforce non-overridable rules and delegate the rest to folder and VPC levels.
questions.distractor_summary: Copied rules can be modified locally, organization policies don't define firewall rules, and Cloud Armor isn't used for internal VPC traffic.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: An internal HR application runs on Cloud Run. It must not be reachable from the internet at all, only from corporate users through an internal Application Load Balancer reached over Cloud Interconnect. What should the architect configure?
options: Set Cloud Run ingress to internal and Cloud Load Balancing only, fronted by an internal ALB.
Keep the default ingress setting and require authentication on every request to the service.
Restrict access with a Cloud Armor policy applied to the default run.app URL endpoint.
Deploy the Cloud Run service in a private VPC subnet with no external IP address.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Run's ingress settings can block direct internet access, while an internal load balancer with a serverless NEG exposes the service privately to connected networks.
questions.distractor_summary: Default ingress allows internet reachability, Cloud Armor can't attach to the default URL, and Cloud Run services aren't deployed into subnets.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A bank is hardening a production GKE platform. Requirements: no public IPs on nodes, Pods authenticate to Google APIs without keys, node boot integrity is verified, and Pod-to-Pod traffic follows least-privilege rules. Which combination should the architect specify?
options: Public nodes with firewall rules, node service account keys, and default Kubernetes networking.
GKE Autopilot with public nodes and Kubernetes RBAC for pod-to-pod traffic control.
Private nodes with Cloud NAT for outbound internet access and default pod networking between pods.
Private nodes, Workload Identity Federation, Shielded GKE with Secure Boot, and NetworkPolicy.
questions.correct_rationale: Private nodes remove public exposure, Workload Identity Federation avoids keys, Shielded nodes verify boot integrity, and network policies restrict Pod traffic.
questions.distractor_summary: The other options leave public exposure, use keys, or omit Pod-level traffic controls.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company with 400 projects wants a single place to detect misconfigurations such as public buckets and open firewall rules, identify vulnerabilities, detect active threats, and prioritize findings across the organization. What should the architect recommend?
options: Separate Cloud Monitoring dashboards configured for each of the 400 projects individually.
Activate Security Command Center (Premium or Enterprise) at the organization level.
Weekly manual audits using gcloud scripts to check for misconfigurations across projects.
VPC Flow Logs enabled in every project with alerts configured for suspicious traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: Security Command Center provides organization-wide posture management, vulnerability findings, and threat detection in one place.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-project dashboards and manual audits don't scale or detect threats, and flow logs are a data source rather than a security posture platform.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: Security Command Center Event Threat Detection reports cryptocurrency mining on Compute Engine VMs a few times a month. The security team wants those VMs isolated automatically within minutes of a finding, with a notification to the on-call team. What should the architect design?
options: Configure SCC notifications to Pub/Sub, triggering a function that isolates the VM and notifies on-call.
Review Security Command Center findings manually each morning and take containment action as needed by the team.
Delete the entire project immediately when any threat detection finding appears.
Disable Event Threat Detection to reduce alert noise and focus on other security signals.
questions.correct_rationale: Finding notifications through Pub/Sub enable automated, fast containment while preserving evidence.
questions.distractor_summary: Daily manual review is too slow, deleting projects destroys evidence and services, and disabling detection hides threats.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: After a supply chain incident, a company wants to ensure that only container images built by its official CI pipeline and approved by security can run on its production GKE clusters and Cloud Run services. What should the architect implement?
options: Kubernetes RBAC restricting which users and service accounts can deploy to production clusters.
Artifact Registry cleanup policies that automatically delete old or unverified images.
Binary Authorization with attestations from CI and security, enforced on production GKE clusters and Cloud Run services.
Private clusters with authorized networks to restrict who can access the Kubernetes API.
questions.correct_rationale: Binary Authorization enforces deploy-time policies that permit only images with required attestations.
questions.distractor_summary: RBAC controls who deploys rather than what is deployed, cleanup policies manage storage, and network controls don't verify image provenance.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A platform team wants to prevent container images with critical vulnerabilities from reaching production, with vulnerabilities detected automatically when images are pushed and continuously as new CVEs are published. What should the architect design?
options: Monthly manual vulnerability scans run on developer laptops before pushing images.
Runtime detection only, scanning containers after they've already been deployed to production environments.
Use only official base images from trusted vendors and skip the vulnerability scanning step.
Enable Artifact Analysis scanning and gate Binary Authorization attestations on scan results in CI.
questions.correct_rationale: Artifact Analysis scans images on push and as new vulnerabilities are published, and gating attestations on scan results blocks vulnerable images.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual scans are infrequent, runtime detection is too late to prevent deployment, and base images can still contain vulnerabilities.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company's security operations center needs to ingest petabytes of logs from Google Cloud, on-premises firewalls, endpoint tools, and SaaS apps; retain them for a year; and run fast threat hunting and detection rules across all sources. What should the architect recommend?
options: Google Security Operations (SIEM) with ingestion from Google Cloud and third-party log sources.
Cloud Logging's _Default log bucket with one-year retention configured at the organization level.
BigQuery tables queried manually by analysts using SQL for threat hunting and detection of incidents.
Cloud Monitoring alerts configured on log-based metrics for security-relevant events in each project.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Security Operations is a cloud SIEM built to ingest multi-source security telemetry at scale with long retention, detection rules, and threat hunting.
questions.distractor_summary: Default log buckets and manual BigQuery queries lack SIEM capabilities, and Monitoring alerts target metrics.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A production VM shows signs of compromise. The incident response team needs to stop further damage while preserving evidence for forensic analysis. What should the architect recommend as initial steps?
options: Delete the compromised VM immediately and recreate it from a known-good machine image.
Isolate the VM with restrictive firewall rules, snapshot disks for forensics, and investigate.
Restart the VM to clear memory and check whether the suspicious behavior stops afterward.
Grant the attacker's IP an allow rule temporarily to track their activity and gather evidence.
questions.correct_rationale: Isolating the VM limits spread, while snapshots and logs preserve evidence for investigation.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting or restarting destroys evidence, and allowing attacker traffic increases risk.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A financial services company must continuously demonstrate compliance with CIS benchmarks across its Google Cloud organization, detect configuration drift, and report posture to auditors. What should the architect recommend?
options: An annual external compliance audit conducted by a third-party security firm with a detailed report.
Custom scripts run manually before each audit to check for configuration drift.
Security Command Center posture management with CIS benchmarks, compliance reporting, and drift findings.
Cloud Billing reports reviewed monthly for unexpected charges or resource changes.
questions.correct_rationale: Security postures in Security Command Center define and monitor benchmark-based controls, detect drift, and support compliance reporting.
questions.distractor_summary: Annual audits and pre-audit scripts don't provide continuous monitoring, and billing reports are unrelated to compliance.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A regulated bank requires visibility into any access to its data by Google personnel and wants the ability to explicitly approve or deny such access before it occurs for supported services. What should the architect enable?
options: Cloud Audit Logs Data Access logs to monitor all access to the bank's data in every project.
VPC Service Controls perimeters around all data projects and storage buckets in the organization.
Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM) with keys held in the bank's own HSM.
Access Transparency logs and Access Approval for Google personnel access control.
questions.correct_rationale: Access Transparency records actions taken by Google personnel on customer content, and Access Approval requires explicit customer approval before such access.
questions.distractor_summary: Data Access logs record customer principals' access, VPC Service Controls restricts API access paths, and EKM controls keys rather than approving personnel access.

questions.domain: 3. Designing for Security and Compliance
questions.question: A company deploys public web applications on App Engine, Compute Engine, and GKE and wants automated scanning of these applications for common vulnerabilities such as cross-site scripting and outdated libraries before and after releases. What should the architect recommend?
options: Cloud Armor security policies running in preview mode to detect common web vulnerabilities.
Web Security Scanner integrated with Security Command Center for automated scanning.
VPC Flow Logs analysis to detect anomalous traffic patterns to public web applications.
Binary Authorization to verify container image provenance before deployment to production.
questions.correct_rationale: Web Security Scanner crawls web applications to identify vulnerabilities such as XSS and outdated libraries and reports findings to Security Command Center.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Armor filters traffic rather than scanning apps, flow logs show network flows, and Binary Authorization controls image deployment.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A retail startup must launch a loyalty program in eight weeks to match a competitor. The engineering team of six proposes building a custom message queue, a custom identity system, and a self-managed database cluster to keep full control. The CEO's top priority is time to market, and the team has limited operations experience. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use managed services like Pub/Sub, Identity Platform, and Cloud SQL to focus on business features.
Build the custom message queue, identity system, and database cluster as originally proposed by the team.
Outsource all development to an external contractor that has Google Cloud experience and certifications.
Build a minimal version on a single VM with no redundancy, no automated scaling, and no monitoring.
questions.correct_rationale: Managed services reduce build and operations effort, aligning with the time-to-market priority and the team's limited operations experience.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom infrastructure delays launch and adds operational risk, outsourcing doesn't address platform choice, and a single VM creates reliability risks for a customer-facing program.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A SaaS company's contract promises customers 99.9% monthly availability with service credits if missed. The engineering team wants to know how to set its internal reliability target. What should the architect recommend?
options: Set the internal SLO equal to the contractual SLA at 99.9% monthly availability for the service.
Set the internal SLO lower than the SLA, at 99.5%, to reduce the engineering effort required to maintain it.
Set an internal SLO stricter than the SLA (for example, 99.95%) to buffer before breaches.
Don't set an internal SLO at all; track only the contractual SLA reported to customers each month.
questions.correct_rationale: An internal SLO tighter than the contractual SLA gives a buffer to detect and fix problems before breaching the agreement.
questions.distractor_summary: Matching the SLA leaves no margin, a looser SLO guarantees breaches, and tracking only the SLA gives no early warning.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: An e-commerce company wants an SLI for its checkout experience that reflects what customers care about: purchases that succeed quickly. Which SLI is most appropriate?
options: Average CPU utilization of the checkout VMs measured over each 24-hour period of operation.
The proportion of checkout requests that return a successful response within 300 ms.
The number of checkout VMs currently running and healthy behind the load balancer at any given time.
Database disk usage percentage as a proxy for checkout system load and health.
questions.correct_rationale: A good SLI measures user-facing outcomes, such as the ratio of successful and fast requests, ideally close to the user at the load balancer.
questions.distractor_summary: CPU, VM counts, and disk usage are internal resource metrics that don't directly reflect customer experience.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A board approved a cloud migration expecting "better agility and lower costs." Twelve months later, the board asks whether the migration succeeded, but no one can answer objectively. What should the architect have established at the start?
options: A list of all migrated servers and their new Google Cloud instance names and zones.
The total number of Google Cloud services adopted across the organization after the migration was completed.
The monthly cloud bill compared against the previous on-premises data center costs.
Measurable KPIs with baselines: deployment frequency, lead time, cost per transaction, availability.
questions.correct_rationale: Defining baseline and target KPIs tied to business goals allows objective evaluation of outcomes such as agility and cost efficiency.
questions.distractor_summary: Server counts and service counts measure activity rather than outcomes, and the bill alone ignores business value and volume changes.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company's steady baseline workload uses about 200 vCPUs around the clock, with seasonal peaks of up to 600 vCPUs for a few weeks a year. The CFO wants predictable spending and discounts, while engineering wants flexibility for peaks. What should the architect recommend?
options: Committed use discounts sized to the steady baseline, with on-demand or Spot capacity for peaks.
Committed use discounts for 600 vCPUs to cover both the steady baseline and the seasonal peak demand.
On-demand pricing only for maximum flexibility and no long-term financial commitment.
Spot VMs for all workloads including the baseline, with automatic migration on preemption.
questions.correct_rationale: Committing to the baseline captures discounts and predictability, while autoscaled on-demand capacity handles temporary peaks.
questions.distractor_summary: Committing to peak capacity wastes money most of the year, on-demand only forgoes discounts, and Spot VMs are unsuitable for interruption-sensitive baseline workloads.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company is modernizing web applications into containers. Its operations team has strong Linux skills but no Kubernetes experience, and leadership wants to start delivering value within one quarter while building skills over time. What should the architect recommend?
options: Build a self-managed Kubernetes cluster on Compute Engine to learn the platform internals.
Delay modernization until the operations team is fully certified in Kubernetes administration.
Start with Cloud Run for stateless services while training the team, adopting GKE later.
Deploy everything to GKE Standard immediately with default settings and learn on the job.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Run delivers containerized services quickly with minimal platform skills, while training prepares the team for GKE when needed.
questions.distractor_summary: Self-managed Kubernetes and immediate GKE Standard adoption add risk given the skills gap, and waiting delays business value.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: An insurance company receives 50,000 claim forms per month as PDFs and scanned images and wants structured data extracted into its claims system. A team proposes collecting labeled data and training a custom OCR model from scratch over six months. What should the architect recommend first?
options: Hire a team of manual data entry specialists to process the claim forms each month.
Evaluate Document AI processors to extract structured fields with minimal custom development.
Train a custom OCR model on Compute Engine GPUs using labeled data collected over six months.
Store the PDFs in Cloud Storage and search them with keyword queries when needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Document AI provides managed document processing that can be adapted to specific forms, reducing time and cost compared with building from scratch.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual entry doesn't scale, a custom OCR model is slow and costly, and keyword search doesn't produce structured data.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A European fintech wants the lowest possible latency for trading users in Singapore, and product managers propose storing customer account data in `asia-southeast1`. However, EU regulations applying to the company require that this personal data stay in the EU. How should the architect resolve the conflict?
options: Store the customer account data in Singapore because latency directly affects trading revenue.
Store data in both regions simultaneously and hope that regulators don't discover the duplication.
Choose the region with the lowest compute and storage costs for the trading platform's workloads.
Treat data residency as a hard constraint; keep personal data in the EU and optimize latency.
questions.correct_rationale: Regulatory requirements are non-negotiable constraints, so the design must optimize latency within them.
questions.distractor_summary: Violating residency for performance or cost creates legal risk, and duplicating data outside the EU still breaches the requirement.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A large enterprise's cloud adoption has stalled: teams use Google Cloud inconsistently, security is ad hoc, and leadership lacks a clear roadmap. The CIO asks the architect how to assess the organization's cloud maturity and plan next steps. What should the architect use?
options: The Google Cloud Adoption Framework, assessing maturity across Learn, Lead, Scale, and Secure.
A list of all Google Cloud services the company doesn't yet use.
A migration plan for all remaining on-premises servers with timelines and dependencies.
A cost-reduction program focused on eliminating unused resources and optimizing spending.
questions.correct_rationale: The Cloud Adoption Framework evaluates people, process, and technology maturity across themes and guides a roadmap.
questions.distractor_summary: A service list or server migration plan doesn't address organizational maturity, and cost reduction alone ignores skills, leadership, and security.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A traditional bank's executives are nervous about moving to the cloud, and several teams resist change. The architect needs to build confidence and demonstrate value early with limited risk. What should the architect recommend?
options: Migrate the core banking system first to demonstrate commitment to the cloud strategy.
Mandate that all teams complete their migration within three months of the announcement.
Select a lighthouse project, deliver it successfully, share lessons, and build patterns.
Wait until competitors have fully migrated before starting the bank's own cloud journey.
questions.correct_rationale: A lighthouse project provides a low-risk, visible success that builds skills, reusable patterns, and organizational confidence.
questions.distractor_summary: Starting with the core system is high risk, mandates fuel resistance, and waiting forfeits advantage.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A customer-facing API depends on three serially dependent components, each with 99.95% availability, and any single failure makes the API unavailable. The business wants to promise 99.95% availability for the API. What should the architect advise?
options: The API's availability is 99.95%, because it matches the 99.95% availability of each of its three components.
The API's availability is the highest of the three serially dependent component availabilities in the chain.
Availability can't be estimated for serially dependent systems without more information.
Expected availability is roughly 99.85% (0.9995³); meeting 99.95% needs redundancy or fewer dependencies.
questions.correct_rationale: Availabilities of serial dependencies multiply, lowering the composite availability below each component's.
questions.distractor_summary: Achieving the target requires redundancy, graceful degradation, or fewer hard dependencies, so the other options misstate how availability composes.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A ticketing company expects traffic to spike to 20 times normal levels when a major concert goes on sale next month. It has never tested at that scale. What should the architect recommend first?
options: Run load tests simulating expected peak traffic, identify bottlenecks, and fix them before the sale.
Double all server resources the night before the sale to handle the expected 20x traffic spike safely.
Rely on autoscaling to handle the traffic spike without any prior load testing or validation of limits.
Enable Cloud CDN for all API calls to reduce the load on the backend application servers during peaks.
questions.correct_rationale: Load testing reveals bottlenecks like database limits, quotas, and scaling delays before real users are affected.
questions.distractor_summary: Blind resource increases may miss the true bottleneck, untested autoscaling can hit limits, and CDN doesn't help with dynamic, personalized API calls.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A news website's Cloud SQL primary is at 95% CPU, driven mainly by repeated reads of the same popular articles. Write volume is low. The team wants to reduce latency and database load without changing the database engine. What should the architect recommend?
options: Scale the Cloud SQL primary vertically to the largest available machine type in the region.
Migrate the database to Cloud Spanner for globally distributed and horizontally scalable reads.
Add Cloud SQL read replicas for read traffic and a Memorystore cache for popular articles.
Increase the Cloud SQL disk size to reduce I/O contention during peak read periods.
questions.correct_rationale: Read replicas offload reads, and caching serves repeated requests from memory, both targeting a read-heavy bottleneck.
questions.distractor_summary: Vertical scaling has limits and cost, Spanner is a major change not justified by read load, and disk size doesn't address CPU.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company's image-processing service on GKE uses far more CPU than expected, raising costs. Engineers suspect inefficient code but don't know which functions are responsible. They want continuous, low-overhead analysis in production. What should the architect recommend?
options: Increase node sizes in the GKE cluster to handle the CPU demand more cost-effectively.
Use Cloud Profiler to continuously profile CPU and memory usage by function in production.
Add more logging statements throughout the code to identify which functions use the most CPU.
Use VPC Flow Logs to analyze network traffic patterns and identify inefficient service calls.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Profiler collects low-overhead CPU and heap profiles from production and shows which functions consume resources.
questions.distractor_summary: Larger nodes increase cost without fixing code, logging doesn't reveal CPU hotspots effectively, and flow logs show network traffic.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: Users report that a request passing through eight microservices sometimes takes more than five seconds. Each team says its own service is fast. The architect needs to find which call contributes the latency. What should the architect use?
options: Cloud Monitoring CPU utilization charts for each of the eight microservices in the request path.
Log-based metrics configured to alert on error rates for each microservice independently of the others.
Uptime checks for each microservice to measure availability and response time individually, per region.
Distributed tracing with Cloud Trace to see per-span latency across all services in the path.
questions.correct_rationale: Distributed tracing follows a request across services and shows the time spent in each span, identifying the slow dependency.
questions.distractor_summary: CPU charts, error metrics, and uptime checks don't reveal where latency accumulates within a request path.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A managed instance group serving a web application takes about four minutes for new VMs to become ready. Every morning, traffic ramps up quickly at 8 AM, and users see errors before the autoscaler catches up. What should the architect recommend?
options: Configure an initialization period and enable predictive autoscaling for the daily traffic ramp.
Disable autoscaling entirely and run at maximum capacity throughout the entire day.
Reduce the autoscaling target utilization to 5% so that new VMs are added more aggressively each day.
Switch to Spot VMs to reduce the cost of running at maximum capacity during low-traffic hours each day.
questions.correct_rationale: Predictive autoscaling uses historical load patterns to scale out before predictable ramps, compensating for long startup times.
questions.distractor_summary: Running at maximum wastes money, an extremely low target is wasteful and still reactive, and Spot VMs don't speed scaling.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company's GKE Standard clusters run at about 30% average node utilization. Many Pods have inflated resource requests, and some batch workloads could tolerate interruptions. The company wants to reduce costs without harming critical services. What should the architect recommend?
options: Buy committed use discounts for the current node count to reduce the hourly compute rate.
Disable the cluster autoscaler and manually manage node count based on expected daily demand patterns.
Rightsize Pod requests with VPA, use optimize-utilization profile, and move batch to Spot pools.
Move all workloads to one large node to reduce the total number of nodes and overhead.
questions.correct_rationale: Accurate requests improve bin-packing, the optimize-utilization profile scales down more aggressively, and Spot nodes reduce costs for tolerant workloads.
questions.distractor_summary: Commitments lock in waste, disabling autoscaling increases idle capacity, and a single node creates reliability risk.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: Executive dashboards in Looker Studio query a 20 TB BigQuery table every few minutes, scanning the full table each time. Costs are high, and dashboards are slow. The dashboards aggregate data by day and region. What should the architect recommend?
options: Increase the dashboards' refresh frequency so users see more up-to-date information.
Create materialized views for the aggregations and consider BI Engine for acceleration.
Export the table to Cloud SQL so dashboards can query a relational database directly.
Duplicate the table for each dashboard so they don't compete for the same scan resources.
questions.correct_rationale: Materialized views precompute aggregations, BI Engine accelerates interactive queries, and column selection with partition filters reduce bytes scanned.
questions.distractor_summary: More refreshes increase cost, Cloud SQL isn't suited to 20 TB analytics, and duplicate tables add cost.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A Cloud Run service scales to several hundred instances during peaks, each opening its own connections to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The database hits its connection limit, causing errors, although CPU remains moderate. What should the architect recommend?
options: Increase the Cloud SQL database's disk size to handle more concurrent connections from Cloud Run.
Remove all maximum instance limits on Cloud Run so that it can scale freely during traffic peaks.
Switch the database to a public IP address to improve connection throughput and latency for Cloud Run.
Introduce connection pooling and limit connections per instance and max Cloud Run instances.
questions.correct_rationale: Pooling multiplexes many client connections over fewer database connections, and limiting instances and per-instance connections keeps totals within database limits.
questions.distractor_summary: Disk size and IP type don't affect connection limits, and removing instance limits makes exhaustion worse.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company maintains 15 small Compute Engine VMs whose only purpose is to run cron scripts once a day, each taking less than 10 minutes. The VMs require patching and cost money around the clock. What should the architect recommend?
options: Package the scripts as containers and run them as Cloud Run jobs triggered by Cloud Scheduler on a schedule.
Consolidate all scripts onto one larger VM to reduce management overhead and cost.
Keep the VMs running and buy committed use discounts to reduce the hourly rate.
Move the scripts to GKE Standard with dedicated nodes for better scheduling and isolation.
questions.correct_rationale: Scheduled Cloud Run jobs eliminate always-on VMs and patching, charging only while jobs run.
questions.distractor_summary: One larger VM still requires management and idle cost, commitments lock in waste, and a dedicated GKE cluster adds overhead for simple jobs.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: An application writes millions of small log objects per hour to a Cloud Storage bucket using names such as `2026-09-30-10-00-00-000001.log`, `2026-09-30-10-00-00-000002.log`. During bursts, the application sees increased latency and occasional request errors from Cloud Storage. What should the architect recommend?
options: Switch the bucket to the Archive storage class to reduce the cost of storing the log objects.
Add a random or hashed prefix to object names to distribute load across the key range.
Enable Object Versioning to protect against accidental deletion of important log objects in the bucket.
Reduce the object size to 1 KB so more objects fit within the same request budget.
questions.correct_rationale: Sequential names concentrate requests on a narrow key range, which can create hotspots during rapid ramps; randomized prefixes spread load.
questions.distractor_summary: Storage class and versioning don't affect request distribution, and smaller objects increase request counts.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A research institute runs thousands of containerized simulation jobs each week, some needing GPUs. Researchers currently create and delete VMs by hand, leaving idle VMs running for days. The institute wants a managed service that queues jobs, provisions the right resources, and cleans up automatically. What should the architect recommend?
options: A permanent GKE Standard cluster sized for peak load and kept running throughout the entire week.
Cloud Run functions for each simulation, triggered on demand by researchers through an HTTP request.
Cloud Scheduler with scripts that create and delete Compute Engine VMs automatically on a schedule.
Batch, which schedules, provisions, and deletes resources for jobs including GPU and Spot VMs.
questions.correct_rationale: Batch is a managed service that queues jobs, provisions VMs with the required resources, and cleans them up after completion.
questions.distractor_summary: A permanent peak-sized cluster wastes capacity, functions have time and resource limits unsuitable for long GPU jobs, and scripts recreate the manual problem.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company has committed to reducing the carbon footprint of its cloud workloads. It runs large batch analytics jobs that aren't latency sensitive and can run in any North American region. What should the architect recommend?
options: Run the jobs in the region closest to company headquarters, regardless of that region's electricity energy mix.
Run the jobs continuously to avoid the emissions associated with frequent startup and shutdown cycles.
Run the jobs in regions with higher carbon-free energy percentage and use Carbon Footprint reporting.
Use larger machine types so the jobs finish faster and consume less total energy over the following months.
questions.correct_rationale: Choosing low-carbon regions for flexible workloads reduces emissions, and Carbon Footprint reporting tracks progress.
questions.distractor_summary: Proximity to headquarters doesn't matter for batch work, continuous running wastes energy, and bigger machines don't necessarily lower emissions.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: During migration planning, an architect finds that an internal reporting application hasn't been used by anyone in 14 months, but it still runs on three on-premises servers with expensive licenses. What migration strategy should the architect recommend for this application?
options: Rehost it to Compute Engine with minimal changes to preserve all of the existing functionality.
Refactor it into microservices to modernize the application architecture and reduce technical debt.
Retire it after confirming with stakeholders, and archive any required data for compliance.
Repurchase a SaaS replacement that provides similar reporting functionality in the cloud.
questions.correct_rationale: Unused applications should be retired, eliminating migration effort and licensing cost, with data archived if retention is required.
questions.distractor_summary: Rehosting, refactoring, or buying a replacement spends money on something no one uses.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company plans to migrate 2,000 on-premises servers and needs to discover inventory, collect utilization data, map dependencies, and estimate Google Cloud costs before building a business case. What should the architect use?
options: Manual spreadsheets filled in by each application owner with server specs and utilization.
Migration Center to discover assets, collect performance data, and generate cost estimates.
Cloud Asset Inventory applied to on-premises servers through a custom connector.
The Pricing Calculator alone, using estimated server specifications from application owners.
questions.correct_rationale: Migration Center discovers and assesses on-premises infrastructure, including utilization, and produces cost and migration planning outputs.
questions.distractor_summary: Spreadsheets are incomplete, Asset Inventory tracks Google Cloud resources, and the Pricing Calculator requires already-known specifications.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: An online retailer must migrate a 3 TB MySQL database from its data center to Cloud SQL for MySQL. The business allows at most 10 minutes of downtime during cutover. What should the architect recommend?
options: Export a mysqldump of the database, import it into Cloud SQL, and cut over to the new instance.
Copy the raw database files to Cloud Storage and restore them manually onto a Cloud SQL instance.
Rebuild the database from application logs and replay them into the new Cloud SQL instance.
Use Database Migration Service with continuous replication, then promote during a short cutover.
questions.correct_rationale: DMS performs an initial load followed by continuous change replication, so cutover requires only a brief promotion.
questions.distractor_summary: A one-time dump and import of 3 TB takes far longer than 10 minutes of downtime, raw file copies aren't a supported migration path to Cloud SQL, and rebuilding from logs is impractical.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company wants to move off an expensive Oracle database to a PostgreSQL-compatible managed database with high performance. It needs help converting schemas and code objects and wants to minimize downtime during migration. What should the architect recommend?
options: Database Migration Service for Oracle to AlloyDB with a conversion workspace and continuous replication.
Rehost Oracle on Compute Engine and keep the existing licenses, patches, and operational processes intact.
Export the Oracle tables to CSV files, then load them into BigQuery for analytical workloads and reports.
Rewrite the entire application for PostgreSQL before migrating any data to the cloud, then test everything.
questions.correct_rationale: DMS supports heterogeneous Oracle migrations to PostgreSQL-compatible targets, with conversion workspaces for schema and code and continuous replication to limit downtime.
questions.distractor_summary: Rehosting keeps licensing costs, BigQuery isn't a transactional replacement, and a full rewrite first delays benefits.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company wants to modernize a large, business-critical monolith into microservices, but a full rewrite is considered too risky. The business must keep shipping features during modernization. What approach should the architect recommend?
options: Freeze all feature development and rewrite the monolith in a single major release cycle.
Rehost the monolith to Compute Engine and never attempt to modernize the architecture.
Apply the strangler fig pattern: route through a facade, extract services incrementally, retire monolith parts.
Split the monolith's database into separate databases first, without changing any application code yet.
questions.correct_rationale: The strangler fig pattern replaces functionality incrementally while the system keeps running, reducing risk and allowing continued delivery.
questions.distractor_summary: A big-bang rewrite is risky, never modernizing ignores the goal, and splitting the database without code changes breaks the application.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company has dozens of Linux-based Java web applications running on VMs. It wants to move them to GKE to standardize operations and improve density, without rewriting code or manually writing Dockerfiles and Kubernetes manifests for each. What should the architect recommend?
options: Rewrite each application as a Cloud Run function and decompose the monolithic architecture.
Use Migrate to Containers to extract applications from VMs into container images and K8s artifacts.
Rehost the VMs on Compute Engine and run kubectl commands on them for container management.
Build Docker container images manually for each application and write Kubernetes manifests by hand.
questions.correct_rationale: Migrate to Containers automates converting VM-based workloads into containers and Kubernetes artifacts, supporting replatforming without rewrites.
questions.distractor_summary: Rewriting as functions is a refactor, rehosting doesn't containerize, and manual builds are slow at this scale.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A retailer is migrating a 200 TB Teradata data warehouse to BigQuery. It has thousands of SQL scripts and reports written in Teradata SQL. What should the architect recommend to reduce migration effort?
options: Rewrite all SQL scripts manually to BigQuery Standard SQL before starting the data migration work.
Keep Teradata running and replicate data to BigQuery indefinitely for dual-running workloads.
Export data to Cloud Storage and query it with BigQuery external tables without migrating logic.
Use BigQuery Migration Service with SQL translator for Teradata SQL and data transfer tooling.
questions.correct_rationale: BigQuery Migration Service provides assessment, SQL translation, and migration tooling that automate much of the conversion.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual rewriting is slow, permanent dual running is costly, and external tables alone don't migrate the warehouse or its logic.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company is planning migration waves for 150 applications. The first wave moved an order application to Google Cloud while its tightly coupled inventory service stayed on-premises. Chatty calls across the hybrid link caused severe latency. How should the architect plan future waves?
options: Use dependency mapping to group tightly coupled applications and move them together in the same wave.
Migrate applications alphabetically by application name to distribute the work evenly across all waves.
Migrate the largest applications first, regardless of their dependencies on other services and data stores.
Add more bandwidth to the hybrid connection and keep the current wave-based migration plan unchanged for now.
questions.correct_rationale: Grouping interdependent applications prevents latency-sensitive calls from crossing hybrid links during the transition.
questions.distractor_summary: Alphabetical or size-based ordering ignores dependencies, and more bandwidth doesn't fix per-call latency for chatty interactions.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company is cutting over its core database from on-premises to Cloud SQL for a weekend. Leadership insists on the ability to roll back to on-premises within hours if serious problems appear in the first days, without losing transactions made in the cloud. What should the architect include in the plan?
options: Delete the on-premises database immediately after confirming that the cutover was successful in production.
Take one backup before cutover and restore it on-premises if serious problems appear in the first days.
Set up reverse replication from Cloud SQL to on-premises, and define rollback criteria and procedures.
Run both databases independently and reconcile any differences between them manually after the first week.
questions.correct_rationale: Reverse replication keeps the old system current so rollback doesn't lose new transactions, and defined criteria make the decision clear.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting the source removes rollback, a pre-cutover backup loses post-cutover data, and independent writes create conflicts.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: A company must migrate 500 TB of files from on-premises NAS to Cloud Storage. Files keep changing during the three-week migration, and cutover downtime must be short. The company has a 10 Gbps Interconnect. What should the architect recommend?
options: Run a single gcloud storage cp command at the start of the migration to copy every one of the files at once.
Storage Transfer Service with on-premises agents for bulk transfer, then incremental syncs at cutover.
Transfer Appliance only for the initial copy, with no incremental updates during the three-week migration.
Email files to the cloud team in batches and upload them manually to Cloud Storage.
questions.correct_rationale: Storage Transfer Service handles large transfers over the available link, and incremental runs capture changes so the final sync is short.
questions.distractor_summary: A single copy misses changes, an appliance alone doesn't capture ongoing changes, and emailing files isn't viable.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
