questions.question: A company runs 800 VMs on VMware vSphere and must exit its data center within four months. Its operations team relies heavily on vCenter, NSX, and existing VMware runbooks, and wants to keep them during the move before modernizing. What should the architect recommend?
options: Refactor all 800 workloads to run on GKE with container-native operational processes.
Convert every VM to Compute Engine images by hand using the Google Cloud console and gcloud command tools.
Retire all VMware workloads and rebuild only the most critical applications in the cloud.
Migrate VMs to Google Cloud VMware Engine using HCX, keeping existing VMware operational processes.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Cloud VMware Engine runs native VMware stacks in Google Cloud, allowing fast migration with existing tools and runbooks.
questions.distractor_summary: Refactoring takes too long, manual conversion is slow and changes operations, and retiring all workloads isn't realistic.

questions.domain: 4. Analyzing and Optimizing Technical and Business Processes
questions.question: Three months after rehosting 300 VMs to Compute Engine with the same sizes they had on-premises, the monthly bill is 40% higher than forecast. Utilization data shows most VMs are heavily overprovisioned. What should the architect recommend?
options: Apply rightsizing recommendations based on observed utilization, then evaluate CUDs for the baseline.
Buy three-year committed use discounts for the current VM sizes to reduce the hourly rate immediately.
Move everything back on-premises to the original data center and revert the migration entirely.
Add more VMs to spread the load and reduce the CPU utilization on each individual instance.
questions.correct_rationale: Post-migration optimization should rightsize based on real utilization before committing, avoiding locking in waste.
questions.distractor_summary: Committing to oversized VMs increases waste, repatriation ignores the fixable cause, and adding VMs increases cost.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: Developers building a Pub/Sub- and Firestore-based application run integration tests against shared cloud projects. Tests are slow, interfere with each other, and generate unnecessary cost. The team wants fast, isolated local testing. What should the architect advise?
options: Give each developer their own personal production project to avoid any test interference between team members.
Use the Pub/Sub and Firestore emulators for local testing, with targeted CI tests against real services.
Skip integration testing entirely and rely on manual testing before each production release of the services.
Mock all Google Cloud client libraries by hand and maintain the mocks as the services evolve over the years.
questions.correct_rationale: Emulators provide fast, isolated, no-cost local testing, while a targeted set of CI tests validates behavior against real services.
questions.distractor_summary: Personal production projects add cost and risk, skipping tests reduces quality, and hand-written mocks often drift from real service behavior.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A bank's security team prohibits storing source code on developer laptops, and onboarding new developers currently takes a week of environment setup. Developers need consistent environments with approved tools and private access to internal repositories. What should the architect recommend?
options: Cloud Shell Editor with IAM access to the company's repositories for browser-based development.
Shared Compute Engine VMs with one shared account used by all developers on the team.
Let developers use personal laptops with full disk encryption and remote wipe enabled.
Cloud Workstations with standardized, admin-managed configurations running inside the company VPC.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Workstations provides managed, consistent development environments in the company's VPC with admin-managed configurations, keeping source code off laptops and speeding onboarding. Cloud Shell Editor offers browser-based access but does not provide customizable, admin-managed environment templates or the same isolation and control.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Shell Editor provides browser-based access but not admin-managed custom environments; shared VMs with one account remove accountability; personal laptops with encryption still place code on endpoints.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: Build pipelines frequently fail due to rate limits when pulling base images from Docker Hub and packages from public npm and Maven repositories. Security also wants a controlled point through which third-party dependencies enter builds. What should the architect recommend?
options: Artifact Registry remote repositories proxying and caching Docker Hub, npm, and Maven for builds.
Increase the number of build retries with exponential backoff to handle transient rate limit errors.
Download packages manually and commit them to Git so builds don't need external registries.
Use a different public registry for each build to distribute the rate limit across several providers.
questions.correct_rationale: Remote repositories cache upstream artifacts, reducing rate-limit failures and providing a governed ingress point for dependencies.
questions.distractor_summary: Retries don't fix rate limits, committing packages to Git bloats repositories, and switching registries doesn't add control.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A product team uses long-lived feature branches that are merged every six weeks, causing painful merge conflicts and big-bang releases. Business stakeholders want to control when features become visible to customers independently of code deployments. What should the architect advise?
options: Lengthen the release cycle to three months to reduce the number of painful merge conflicts for the teams.
Require a single senior developer to integrate all of the feature branches into the main branch by hand.
Adopt trunk-based development with small merges, and use feature flags to decouple deploy from release.
Deploy directly from developers' laptops to avoid the overhead of a formal release pipeline process entirely.
questions.correct_rationale: Trunk-based development reduces merge conflicts, and feature flags let the business decide when features go live without redeploying.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer cycles worsen integration pain, a single integrator becomes a bottleneck, and laptop deployments bypass controls.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A company runs a web application on a managed instance group behind a global external Application Load Balancer. It needs releases with instant rollback and the ability to test the new version in production-like conditions before switching all traffic. What deployment strategy should the architect recommend?
options: Rolling update with maxUnavailable set to 100% to replace all of the instances at the same time.
Blue/green deployment with two MIGs, switching the URL map after validation and back if needed.
Recreate all instances in place during a scheduled maintenance window on weekends or holiday periods.
Deploy directly on running VMs using SSH scripts and a manual restart of the web server processes.
questions.correct_rationale: Blue/green keeps the old environment running, so traffic can be switched after testing and switched back instantly.
questions.distractor_summary: Replacing everything at once, recreating in place, or patching live VMs doesn't provide instant rollback.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A logistics company exposes a public API to hundreds of partner integrations. The team needs to make breaking changes to response formats but can't force all partners to update at once. What should the architect advise?
options: Change the existing API in place and notify all partners after the change is deployed.
Freeze the API contract forever and never make any breaking changes to the response formats at all.
Maintain separate deployments for each partner with customized response formats per integration.
Introduce a new API version for breaking changes, keep v1 stable with a deprecation timeline.
questions.correct_rationale: Explicit versioning with a deprecation policy lets partners migrate on their own schedule while enabling evolution.
questions.distractor_summary: In-place breaking changes cause outages, freezing blocks progress, and per-partner deployments are unmanageable.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A team deploys application updates with rolling updates on GKE, so old and new versions run simultaneously for several minutes. A new release requires renaming a database column, and the last attempt broke old Pods during the rollout. What should the architect advise?
options: Use the expand-and-contract pattern: add new column, write to both, deploy code, backfill, remove old.
Rename the column during the deployment and accept that some errors will occur during the rollout period.
Stop all traffic to the application during every schema change to avoid version conflicts.
Store all data as JSON blobs in a single column to avoid database schema changes entirely.
questions.correct_rationale: Expand-and-contract keeps the schema compatible with both old and new code during rollouts, enabling zero-downtime changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Accepting errors or stopping traffic hurts users, and abandoning schemas creates other data quality problems.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: Fifty development teams each build their own deployment pipelines, logging setups, and GKE configurations, leading to inconsistent security and slow onboarding. Platform leadership wants teams to move fast while following standards. What should the architect recommend?
options: Mandate a comprehensive 200-page standards document that all teams must read and follow.
Let each team continue building their own pipelines and configurations independently without any oversight.
Build golden paths through an internal developer platform with reusable templates and security built in.
Centralize all deployments through one operations team that reviews every change before release.
questions.correct_rationale: Golden paths make the secure, standard approach the easiest one, improving consistency and speed.
questions.distractor_summary: Documents alone are often ignored, full independence perpetuates inconsistency, and centralizing all deployments creates bottlenecks.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A company's Cloud Build pipelines must deploy to private GKE clusters with no public control plane endpoint and pull dependencies from an on-premises artifact server over Interconnect. Default Cloud Build workers can't reach these private resources. What should the architect recommend?
options: Enable public endpoints on the GKE clusters so Cloud Build can reach them over the internet.
Use Cloud Build private pools peered with the VPC so builds can reach private resources.
Run builds on developers' laptops over VPN connections to the corporate network.
Copy the on-premises artifact server contents to a public Cloud Storage bucket for builds.
questions.correct_rationale: Private pools run build workers in a Google-managed network connected to your VPC, enabling access to private endpoints and hybrid resources.
questions.distractor_summary: Public endpoints and public buckets increase exposure, and laptop builds lose consistency and control.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A software vendor's enterprise customers require verifiable evidence of how each container image was built, including the source revision and build steps, aligned with SLSA. What should the architect advise the development team to implement?
options: Include a README file in each container image describing the build process and source revision used to build it.
Store build logs on a shared drive that enterprise customers can access to verify the whole build process.
Tag images with the developer's name and the date and time they were built, for traceability by customers.
Build with Cloud Build generating signed provenance, store in Artifact Registry, share with customers.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Build can generate signed SLSA build provenance describing the source and build process, which customers can verify.
questions.distractor_summary: README files, logs on shared drives, and name tags aren't tamper-resistant or verifiable.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A data ingestion service calls several Google Cloud APIs at high volume and occasionally receives HTTP 429 and 503 errors. The current code retries immediately in a tight loop, which worsens the problem. What should the architect advise?
options: Retry immediately up to 100 times in a tight loop until the request succeeds or quota resets.
Fail the request permanently on the first error and return an error to the calling application.
Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter, respect retry limits, and ensure idempotency.
Request unlimited quota from Google Cloud support to eliminate rate limiting entirely.
questions.correct_rationale: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries over time and reduces contention, and idempotency makes retries safe.
questions.distractor_summary: Tight retry loops amplify overload, failing immediately loses transient-recoverable work, and unlimited quota isn't available.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A service must call a third-party shipping API that allows at most 50 requests per second. Requests are generated in bursts of thousands, and each must eventually be delivered with retries. What should the architect advise?
options: Enqueue requests in Cloud Tasks with a max dispatch rate and retry policy targeting an HTTP handler.
Publish requests to Pub/Sub with push delivery and no rate control on the subscription.
Call the API directly from each request handler as fast as possible without any queuing or rate control.
Store requests in Cloud Storage and process them manually in batches during off-peak hours each night.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Tasks provides explicit dispatch rate limits and retries per task, matching strict rate limits on downstream APIs.
questions.distractor_summary: Pub/Sub push without rate control can exceed the limit, direct calls cause throttling, and manual processing doesn't scale.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A new customer-facing platform is scheduled for go-live in two weeks. Features are complete, but the operations team hasn't seen the system, and no one has tested failover or load. What should the architect require before approving go-live?
options: Launch as scheduled and address any operational issues as they arise after go-live, without a formal review.
A production readiness review covering load tests, failover, security, monitoring, runbooks, and on-call.
A final demo to executives showing all of the key features working in the staging environment before launch.
A code freeze with no other activities in the two weeks before the scheduled launch date for maximum stability.
questions.correct_rationale: A readiness review verifies that the system can be operated reliably and securely, including tested failure scenarios and prepared operators.
questions.distractor_summary: Launching without readiness risks outages, demos don't prove operability, and a code freeze alone doesn't address operational gaps.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: Two years after a system was built, new engineers keep questioning why it uses Bigtable instead of BigQuery and regional rather than multi-regional deployment. No one remembers the reasoning, and teams waste time relitigating decisions. What should the architect have put in place?
options: Architecture Decision Records documenting context, options, rationale, and consequences per decision.
Comments in the Terraform code explaining why each resource and module was chosen over other options.
A single architecture diagram maintained in the company's internal documentation wiki.
Meeting recordings of all design discussions stored in the company's video platform.
questions.correct_rationale: ADRs capture why decisions were made and what trade-offs were accepted, providing durable, searchable context.
questions.distractor_summary: Code comments and diagrams show what exists rather than why, and recordings are hard to search.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: Before launch, a security team plans a penetration test of the company's applications running on Google Cloud. A manager believes they must first obtain written approval from Google. What should the architect advise?
options: Google must approve all penetration tests in advance through a formal written request and review process.
Penetration tests are prohibited on Google Cloud and will result in suspension of the account or project.
No advance notification to Google is required for testing your own projects if you follow AUP and ToS.
Tests may only be performed by Google employees or by authorized Google security partners and contractors.
questions.correct_rationale: Google doesn't require customers to notify it before penetration testing their own resources, provided they follow the AUP and terms and don't target other customers or Google infrastructure.
questions.distractor_summary: The other statements are incorrect.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A team wants to validate that each release can handle 50,000 concurrent users before promotion to production. It needs a scalable, repeatable load test that runs as part of the release pipeline against a staging environment. What should the architect recommend?
options: Ask employees to use the application simultaneously during a scheduled company-wide test event.
Run a load testing tool from a single developer laptop that is connected to the staging environment.
Test against the production environment during peak hours to validate real-world performance.
Run distributed load tests (e.g., Locust on GKE) from the pipeline with pass/fail thresholds.
questions.correct_rationale: Distributed load generation on GKE can scale to realistic traffic, and pipeline thresholds make results actionable and repeatable.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual tests and single laptops can't generate enough load, and testing production at peak risks customer impact.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: QA teams want production-like data in staging to reproduce real issues, but production data contains customer PII governed by privacy regulations. What should the architect recommend?
options: Copy production data to staging as-is and restrict access to authorized QA team members only.
Create de-identified staging datasets using Sensitive Data Protection masking, tokenization, or date shifting.
Use only tiny hand-written synthetic datasets that don't reflect real production data patterns at all in any way.
Give QA team members direct read access to the production database for debugging issues.
questions.correct_rationale: De-identification produces realistic data for testing without exposing PII, and techniques like deterministic tokenization preserve relationships.
questions.distractor_summary: Raw copies and production access create privacy risk, and tiny synthetic data often misses real-world issues.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: Twelve teams independently release microservices that call each other's APIs. Integration failures are frequently discovered only in production when a provider changes a response field that a consumer depends on. What should the architect recommend?
options: Consumer-driven contract testing in each service's CI pipeline to catch breaking changes at build time.
A monthly full end-to-end test of all twelve microservices deployed together in staging.
Freeze all API changes across all teams and require a formal review board for any modifications.
Merge all services into one repository and release them together as a single deployable monolithic unit.
questions.correct_rationale: Contract tests catch breaking changes at build time without requiring all services to be deployed together.
questions.distractor_summary: Monthly end-to-end tests find problems too late, freezing APIs blocks evolution, and a single release reintroduces monolithic coupling.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A development team is handing over a new payment service to a central SRE team for operation. The SRE team refuses to accept it without better operational documentation. What should the architect ensure is delivered?
options: Only the source code repository link and a brief README with build instructions.
A list of team members' phone numbers and email addresses for emergency escalation during any incidents.
Runbooks for common alerts, architecture docs, SLOs, dashboards, escalation paths, and backup procedures.
A user manual for customers describing the payment service's features, API endpoints, and usage examples.
questions.correct_rationale: Operational documentation such as runbooks, SLOs, dependencies, escalation paths, and recovery procedures enables another team to run the service safely.
questions.distractor_summary: Source code and contact lists aren't operational guidance, and customer manuals don't cover operations.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A platform team publishes shared Terraform modules used by 40 application teams. A recent module change passed code review but broke network configurations for several teams when they upgraded. What should the architect recommend to improve module readiness?
options: Stop versioning modules so all teams always get the latest version automatically on their next apply run.
Allow only the platform team to use the shared modules, while the application teams write their own modules.
Require manual testing by each of the 40 consuming teams before any module change is merged to main branch.
Add automated module tests with terraform test, publish semantic versions, and let teams pin versions.
questions.correct_rationale: Automated testing in ephemeral environments catches breaking changes before release, and semantic versioning with pinning lets consumers upgrade deliberately.
questions.distractor_summary: Unversioned modules spread breaking changes, restricting use defeats the purpose, and manual testing by every team is inefficient.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A release passed all tests in staging but failed in production because production used a different Cloud SQL tier, different firewall rules, and a manually added configuration flag. What should the architect recommend?
options: Test only in production from now on to catch environment-specific differences early.
Define staging and production from the same IaC modules with environment-specific variables and drift detection.
Make staging smaller to save costs regardless of configuration differences between the two environments.
Add more manual steps to the production deployment checklist to catch configuration drift.
questions.correct_rationale: Shared IaC with explicit parameters and drift detection keeps environments consistent, so staging results predict production behavior.
questions.distractor_summary: Testing only in production is risky, unmanaged differences undermine testing, and manual steps introduce more drift.

questions.domain: 5. Managing Implementation
questions.question: A company is launching a new recommendation feature that will call a new backend service for every page view. The team is unsure whether the backend can handle full production traffic and wants to validate it with real traffic before users see the feature. What should the architect recommend?
options: Launch to 100% of users immediately and monitor for errors in production after the release.
Test with synthetic traffic in the development environment to validate backend capacity limits.
Delay the launch until the next major release cycle to allow more time for capacity planning.
A dark launch: send real production requests to the backend in the background to measure performance.
questions.correct_rationale: Dark launches expose the backend to real production load without affecting user experience, revealing capacity issues safely.
questions.distractor_summary: Immediate full launch risks user-facing failures, synthetic development tests may not represent production, and delaying doesn't validate readiness.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: An on-call team receives dozens of pages per week from alerts on high CPU and memory on individual VMs, but most pages don't correspond to any customer impact. Meanwhile, a real outage last month was noticed first by customers. The service has a 99.9% availability SLO. What alerting approach should the architect recommend?
options: Lower CPU alert thresholds so issues are caught earlier before customers notice any impact.
Add more resource-level alerts for disk usage and network throughput on every production VM in the fleet.
Alert on SLO error budget burn rate with fast and slow windows; move resource metrics to dashboards.
Remove all alerts and rely entirely on customer reports to identify service availability issues quickly.
questions.correct_rationale: Burn-rate alerts page only when user-facing reliability is at risk, catching real outages quickly while ignoring harmless resource spikes.
questions.distractor_summary: Lower thresholds and more resource alerts increase noise, and relying on customers delays response.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A company wants to track a service's 99.95% availability SLO over a rolling 28-day window, visualize remaining error budget, and alert when the budget is being consumed too quickly, using Google Cloud's native tools. What should the architect configure?
options: Define the service and SLO in Cloud Monitoring using load balancer metrics as the SLI, with burn-rate alerts.
Export logs to BigQuery and calculate availability manually each month using SQL queries and custom reporting scripts.
Create an uptime check for the service only and track availability through the uptime check dashboard each month.
Build a spreadsheet that on-call engineers update by hand each week to track error budget consumption for the service.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Monitoring's SLO monitoring computes SLI compliance and error budget over rolling windows and supports burn-rate alerts.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual BigQuery calculations and spreadsheets are slow and error-prone, and an uptime check alone doesn't track an error budget from real user traffic.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: An SRE team is overwhelmed by 300 alerts per day, many of which are duplicates or informational. Engineers have started ignoring pages, and burnout is high. What should the architect recommend?
options: Hire more on-call engineers to handle the high volume of alerts and reduce individual team workload significantly.
Page for every alert, but only during business hours, to reduce after-hours disruption for the on-call team members.
Mute all alerts for a full month to give the team a break from the constant notification noise and alert fatigue.
Review alerts: page only for urgent user-impacting symptoms, route others to tickets, deduplicate, delete noise.
questions.correct_rationale: Good alerting pages only for actionable, urgent symptoms, which reduces fatigue and improves response to real incidents.
questions.distractor_summary: More engineers don't fix noisy alerts, business-hours paging ignores real incidents at night, and muting everything hides outages.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A team launching a new user-facing API asks which signals they should put on their primary service dashboard to quickly understand its health. What should the architect recommend?
options: VM uptime percentage and the number of deployments per day or per week for each service owner.
The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation for the primary dashboard.
Only CPU utilization across all VMs and containers running the user-facing API service in production.
Daily cloud cost and the number of log entries generated per hour by the application.
questions.correct_rationale: The golden signals capture user experience (latency, errors) along with demand and resource pressure (traffic, saturation).
questions.distractor_summary: VM uptime, CPU alone, cost, and log counts give an incomplete view of service health.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: Developers struggle to find application exceptions buried in millions of log lines from Cloud Run and GKE services. They want new error types grouped automatically, with counts, stack traces, first-seen times, and notifications. What should the architect recommend?
options: Increase log retention to 90 days so developers can search further back for exceptions.
Create one log-based metric per possible exception type that might occur in the services.
Use Error Reporting to aggregate errors from logs and notify on new error groups automatically.
Enable VPC Flow Logs to capture network traffic patterns that might indicate application errors.
questions.correct_rationale: Error Reporting groups similar exceptions, tracks occurrences and stack traces, and notifies on new errors.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer retention doesn't organize errors, predefining metrics for unknown exceptions isn't feasible, and flow logs don't capture application errors.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: An e-commerce company's uptime checks show the homepage is up, yet customers occasionally can't complete checkout because a login-to-cart-to-payment flow breaks. The company wants to detect broken multi-step user journeys proactively. What should the architect recommend?
options: Cloud Monitoring synthetic monitors running scripted multi-step journeys on a schedule with alerts.
More uptime checks on the homepage and other top-level pages of the e-commerce site.
CPU alerts on the payment servers and login service to detect performance degradation early in advance.
Quarterly manual testing of the checkout flow by the QA team during scheduled test windows.
questions.correct_rationale: Synthetic monitors run scripted tests that exercise critical user flows end to end and alert when they fail.
questions.distractor_summary: Homepage checks don't validate deeper flows, CPU metrics don't prove functionality, and quarterly testing is far too infrequent.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: The security team wants an immediate alert whenever anyone grants the Owner role on any production project. The event appears in Cloud Audit Logs. What should the architect configure?
options: A daily report of IAM policies across all production projects, sent by email to the whole security team.
A CPU-based alerting policy that fires when IAM API usage exceeds a normal baseline threshold for the org.
An uptime check against the IAM API to detect changes in availability or response time of the service.
A log-based alerting policy matching SetIamPolicy entries adding roles/owner, notified to security.
questions.correct_rationale: Log-based alerting policies trigger on matching log entries, enabling near-real-time notification of specific audit events.
questions.distractor_summary: Daily reports are delayed, and CPU alerts or uptime checks don't detect IAM changes.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A company runs workloads on Google Cloud and AWS. Its SRE team wants a single operations view in Cloud Monitoring that includes metrics from EC2 instances and other AWS services alongside Google Cloud resources. What should the architect recommend?
options: Build separate dashboards in each cloud provider and switch between them during incidents.
Configure Cloud Monitoring to collect AWS metrics through an AWS connector project and Ops Agent.
Export AWS logs to Cloud Storage weekly and analyze them alongside Google Cloud data in BigQuery.
Use VPC Flow Logs for AWS instances to capture network traffic in the unified operations view.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Monitoring can ingest AWS metrics through an AWS connector, and the Ops Agent can collect guest-level telemetry, providing a unified view.
questions.distractor_summary: Separate dashboards fragment operations, weekly exports aren't real-time monitoring, and VPC Flow Logs are a Google Cloud feature.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: During an outage, engineers spent an hour debugging their own application before discovering that a Google Cloud service in their region was experiencing an incident. The company wants to be notified automatically about Google Cloud incidents that affect its projects. What should the architect configure?
options: Subscribe engineers to a general cloud news newsletter for updates on service disruptions.
Check the public status dashboard manually during every incident to see provider issues.
Personalized Service Health with alerts for incidents affecting the company's projects and services.
Increase logging verbosity across all services to capture more diagnostic information in incidents.
questions.correct_rationale: Personalized Service Health reports Google Cloud incidents relevant to your projects and can send alerts, shortening diagnosis.
questions.distractor_summary: Newsletters and manual dashboard checks are slow and generic, and more logging doesn't reveal provider incidents.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A product team keeps shipping features rapidly, but its service has exhausted its quarterly error budget after several release-related incidents. Product managers want to keep releasing at the same pace. What should the architect recommend according to SRE practices?
options: Lower the SLO target so that the error budget isn't exhausted by the current release cadence and pace of delivery.
Apply the error budget policy: pause non-essential releases and prioritize reliability work until back in budget.
Ignore the error budget until the next quarter and continue releasing at the current pace of delivery for the product.
Double the release frequency to fix bugs faster and restore the error budget more quickly.
questions.correct_rationale: An error budget policy balances velocity and reliability; when the budget is spent, teams shift effort to reliability.
questions.distractor_summary: Lowering the SLO to fit poor performance undermines its purpose, ignoring the budget makes it meaningless, and more releases increase risk.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A company deploys to GKE through Cloud Deploy using canary rollouts. Last week, a faulty canary ran for hours before someone noticed elevated errors. The company wants canaries to be evaluated and rolled back automatically. What should the architect recommend?
options: Increase the canary percentage to 50% so problems are detected faster during the rollout.
Remove canary stages entirely to speed up the deployment pipeline and reduce complexity.
Ask engineers to watch dashboards during every rollout to catch elevated error rates manually in real time.
Configure deployment verification checking metrics during canary, with automated rollback on failure.
questions.correct_rationale: Automated verification against SLO-related metrics catches bad canaries quickly, and automation can roll back without human delay.
questions.distractor_summary: A larger canary increases impact, removing canaries removes protection, and manual watching is unreliable.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A global outage occurred when a configuration change, a new feature flag value, was pushed to all regions at once. Application code releases already use progressive rollouts, but configuration changes don't. What should the architect recommend?
options: Treat configuration changes like code: roll out progressively by region or percentage with rollback.
Prohibit all configuration changes to eliminate the risk of global outages from bad configuration pushes.
Push configuration changes only on weekends when traffic is lower and impact is reduced.
Store configuration in environment variables baked into container images at build time.
questions.correct_rationale: Progressive, validated rollouts limit the blast radius of configuration changes, just as they do for code.
questions.distractor_summary: Banning changes blocks the business, weekend pushes don't reduce blast radius, and baking configuration into images removes the flexibility of runtime flags.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: Thirty minutes after a release, error rates rise sharply. The on-call engineer thinks they know the bug and wants to write and deploy a fix. The previous version is known to be healthy and can be restored in two minutes. What should the architect recommend as the default practice?
options: Deploy the new fix immediately without testing to restore service as quickly as possible.
Wait until the next business day to decide on a course of action during the active production incident.
Roll back to the last known-good version first to restore service, then investigate and fix.
Scale up the new version to handle the increased error rate and reduce user impact.
questions.correct_rationale: Rolling back to a known-good release mitigates user impact fastest and with the least risk, leaving time for proper diagnosis.
questions.distractor_summary: Untested fixes can make things worse, waiting prolongs the outage, and scaling doesn't fix bugs.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A company releases once per quarter with hundreds of changes per release, and each release causes multi-day incidents. Leadership fears that releasing more often would increase instability. What should the architect advise?
options: Release even less often, twice a year, to reduce the frequency of deployment-related disruptions.
Move toward smaller, more frequent releases with automated testing and progressive delivery.
Require executive sign-off for every change to ensure quality and reduce the risk of failures.
Freeze development until all known bugs are fixed and the codebase is fully stabilized.
questions.correct_rationale: Smaller releases reduce risk per change, simplify troubleshooting, and, with automation, improve both speed and stability as measured by DORA metrics.
questions.distractor_summary: Less frequent releases make batches larger and riskier, heavy approvals slow delivery without improving quality, and freezes halt value delivery.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: During GKE node upgrades and application rollouts, a critical service sometimes has all its replicas terminated at once, and traffic reaches Pods that haven't finished starting. What should the architect recommend?
options: Disable node upgrades entirely to prevent disruption to running workloads during maintenance.
Run a single replica of the critical service to simplify operations and reduce complexity.
Increase the node pool size only to ensure there's always capacity during upgrades and rolling deployments.
Configure PodDisruptionBudgets and readiness probes to keep replicas available during disruptions.
questions.correct_rationale: PodDisruptionBudgets limit simultaneous voluntary evictions, and readiness probes prevent routing to Pods that aren't ready.
questions.distractor_summary: Disabling upgrades leaves clusters unpatched, a single replica removes redundancy, and more nodes don't control eviction behavior.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.subdomain: 6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
questions.question: During a recent major outage, ten engineers debugged simultaneously, customers received conflicting updates, and nobody tracked decisions. What should the architect recommend for future incidents?
options: Adopt structured incident management with defined roles, a shared incident document, and status updates.
Have the most senior engineer handle everything alone to avoid confusion during major incidents.
Let everyone work independently and share results at the end of the incident resolution process entirely.
Wait for the problem to resolve itself before communicating anything to customers or stakeholders.
questions.correct_rationale: Clear incident roles coordinate response, separate communication from debugging, and maintain a record of decisions.
questions.distractor_summary: One person doing everything becomes a bottleneck, uncoordinated work causes confusion, and silence damages customer trust.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.subdomain: 6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
questions.question: After an outage caused by a misconfigured load balancer, management wants to find who made the mistake and discipline them. The architect is concerned this will discourage honest reporting. What should the architect recommend?
options: Publicly identify the engineer responsible to set an example and discourage future mistakes.
Skip the review entirely to avoid conflict and maintain team morale after the infrastructure incident occurred recently.
Conduct a blameless postmortem focusing on timeline, contributing factors, and systemic fixes with tracked actions.
Add more manual approvals to all infrastructure changes to prevent similar misconfigurations.
questions.correct_rationale: Blameless postmortems encourage candor and focus on improving systems and processes so similar failures don't recur.
questions.distractor_summary: Blame discourages reporting, skipping reviews loses learning, and blanket manual approvals slow delivery without addressing root causes.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.subdomain: 6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
questions.question: A global bank running mission-critical workloads on Google Cloud needs the fastest response times for critical issues, proactive guidance, and a named technical contact who knows its architecture. Which support option should the architect recommend?
options: Basic support with community forums and public documentation for self-service troubleshooting.
Premium Support with fastest response for critical cases and a dedicated Technical Account Manager.
Standard Support only with business-hours response times for all severity levels of support cases filed.
Relying on public documentation and community resources for issue resolution and guidance.
questions.correct_rationale: Premium Support offers the fastest critical-case response and a dedicated Technical Account Manager for proactive guidance.
questions.distractor_summary: Basic and Standard support don't provide those response levels or a named contact, and documentation isn't support.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.subdomain: 6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
questions.question: A production outage appears to be caused by unexpected behavior in a Google Cloud managed service. The engineer opening a support case wants it resolved as quickly as possible. What should the case include?
options: A single sentence saying the service is broken without any additional context or details.
Only a screenshot of the Google Cloud console showing the affected service's status page.
Credentials so that support engineers can log in to the company's accounts and investigate the issue directly.
Priority reflecting business impact, project IDs, timestamps, errors, repro steps, and prior troubleshooting.
questions.correct_rationale: Detailed, specific information about impact, resources, timing, errors, and prior troubleshooting lets support diagnose quickly.
questions.distractor_summary: Vague descriptions and screenshots slow resolution, and sharing credentials violates security practices.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.subdomain: 6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
questions.question: An SRE team spends about 70% of its time on repetitive manual tasks such as restarting stuck jobs, rotating certificates by hand, and resizing disks, leaving little time for engineering improvements. What should the architect recommend?
options: Accept the toil as a normal part of operations and plan staffing accordingly for the workload.
Hire external contractors to perform the manual repetitive tasks and free up the SRE team.
Reduce monitoring coverage so fewer alerts and tasks are generated for the on-call team.
Identify and automate high-volume toil (auto-remediation, managed certs, autoscaling) and cap toil time.
questions.correct_rationale: SRE practice limits toil (commonly to under 50% of time) and invests in automation that eliminates repetitive work.
questions.distractor_summary: Accepting or outsourcing toil doesn't reduce it, and less monitoring hides problems rather than resolving them.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.subdomain: 6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
questions.question: A microservices platform is designed to tolerate dependency failures with retries, timeouts, and fallbacks, but these mechanisms have never been exercised. The architect wants confidence that the system behaves as designed when dependencies fail. What should the architect recommend?
options: Wait for a real production outage to validate whether the resilience mechanisms actually work.
Review the code once more to verify that retries, timeouts, and fallbacks are correctly implemented everywhere.
Run controlled chaos experiments injecting latency and errors, starting in staging with abort conditions.
Increase replica counts across all services to provide more redundancy during dependency failures.
questions.correct_rationale: Chaos engineering verifies resilience mechanisms under controlled failure conditions, revealing gaps before real incidents.
questions.distractor_summary: Waiting for outages is risky, code review can't prove runtime behavior, and more replicas don't test fallback logic.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.subdomain: 6.3 Supporting deployed solutions and incident management
questions.question: A company documented a regional disaster recovery plan with an RTO of one hour, but it has never been executed. Auditors ask for evidence that the RTO is achievable. What should the architect recommend?
options: Provide the written DR plan document as evidence that the RTO is achievable and well-documented.
Schedule regular DR drills that perform failover, measure achieved RTO/RPO, and update runbooks based on findings.
Increase the documented RTO to four hours to provide more margin for recovery operations and reduce team pressure.
Assume that managed services handle disaster recovery automatically without any manual intervention.
questions.correct_rationale: Only exercised failovers prove that recovery objectives can be met and reveal gaps in runbooks and automation.
questions.distractor_summary: A document isn't evidence of capability, changing the target avoids the question, and managed services don't automatically fail over entire applications.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A company's defect escape rate to production is high. Code reviews are inconsistent, and tests are run manually when engineers remember. What should the architect recommend to improve quality control?
options: Add a manual QA sign-off at the end of each quarter to review the overall quality of releases.
Rely on production monitoring and alerting to catch defects after they reach live customer traffic.
Reduce the number of tests to speed up builds and allow engineers to focus on feature development work instead.
Enforce automated quality gates in CI: required tests, static analysis, vulnerability scanning, code review.
questions.correct_rationale: Automated quality gates catch defects consistently before changes reach production.
questions.distractor_summary: Quarterly manual sign-off is too late and infrequent, monitoring detects problems after users are affected, and fewer tests reduce coverage.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: After six months of reliability initiatives, leadership asks whether the investments have improved operations. What should the architect use to evaluate this objectively?
options: Trends in SLO attainment, error budget consumption, incident frequency, MTTD, and MTTR vs. baseline.
The number of new monitoring dashboards created and the volume of alerts configured per service across the org.
The number of engineers currently on the SRE team compared with the previous quarter's headcount.
The total number of alerts sent to the on-call rotation over the past six-month period.
questions.correct_rationale: Outcome metrics like SLO attainment, incident rates, and detection and recovery times show whether reliability improved.
questions.distractor_summary: Dashboard counts, headcount, and alert volume measure activity rather than results.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: Deployments complete successfully in the pipeline, but twice this month the newly deployed service was broken because of a missing secret, discovered only when customers complained. What should the architect add to the release process?
options: Longer deployment timeouts to give the service more time to start up and initialize properly.
A manual customer survey after each release to ask whether the service is working correctly.
Automated post-deployment smoke tests exercising critical endpoints, failing the release and triggering rollback.
Deploy less frequently to reduce the number of opportunities for missing secrets to reach production environments.
questions.correct_rationale: Smoke tests verify that the deployed service actually works, catching configuration errors like missing secrets before customers are affected.
questions.distractor_summary: Timeouts don't validate functionality, surveys are slow, and less frequent deployment doesn't prevent the issue.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A service runs in two regions, each normally using about 70% of its capacity. The business requires the service to keep meeting its SLO if one region fails. The architect is reviewing capacity plans. What should the architect conclude?
options: The current capacity is sufficient because average utilization is below 100% in both regions normally.
The plan is insufficient: if one region fails, the other needs ~140% capacity, so N+1 headroom is required.
Capacity planning isn't needed with autoscaling since it automatically adjusts to handle any load increase.
Reduce each region to 50% capacity to save money and let autoscaling handle traffic increases when needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Surviving the loss of one region requires the remaining region to carry the full load, so headroom, autoscaling limits, and quotas must support it.
questions.distractor_summary: Average utilization below 100% doesn't guarantee failover capacity, autoscaling is bounded by quotas and capacity, and reducing capacity worsens the problem.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: An e-commerce homepage fails completely whenever the personalized recommendations service is slow or down, even though customers could still browse and buy without recommendations. What design change should the architect recommend?
options: Make the recommendations service run on a single large VM to improve its reliability and performance under load.
Increase the homepage timeout to 60 seconds so the recommendations service has more time to respond.
Remove the recommendations feature entirely to eliminate the dependency and improve page reliability.
Implement graceful degradation: tight timeouts, circuit breaker, and fallback to cached or default content.
questions.correct_rationale: Graceful degradation keeps core functionality available when non-critical dependencies fail, and circuit breakers prevent cascading slowdowns.
questions.distractor_summary: A larger VM doesn't remove the dependency, longer timeouts worsen user experience, and removing the feature sacrifices value.

questions.domain: 6. Ensuring Solution and Operations Reliability
questions.question: A company's platform has grown over three years, and leadership wants a structured, periodic review to identify reliability, security, cost, and operational gaps against Google-recommended practices. What should the architect use?
options: Review the architecture against the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework pillars and track remediation.
Review only the monthly cloud bill to identify cost optimization opportunities across the entire platform.
Ask each team whether they think their service is fine and collect feedback through a survey.
Replace the platform every three years to ensure it stays current with best practices and new services.
questions.correct_rationale: The Well-Architected Framework provides structured best-practice guidance across pillars, supporting systematic reviews and prioritized improvements.
questions.distractor_summary: Bill reviews cover only cost, self-assessment without a framework is inconsistent, and periodic replacement is wasteful.
